There are some charming foliage hats to be encountered this season in an afternoon's walk, and one which excited my warmest admiration recently was composed of foliage and Chantilly lace, all skilfully intermingled with the most charming result imaginable. As is the case in so many of the best and most fascinating samples of millinery a charming effect was given by a velvet bow at the back of a rather darker shade than the foliage, the result being altogether vdmirable. Chantilly lace plays rather a prominent part in many of the prettiest hats this season, and a quaint sample I recently viewed respectfully as it reposed on the well-dressed coiffure of one of the best-dressed women in London, favoured the Marie • Antoinette shape. It was enveloped in Chantilly lace of the best description, which fell in a picturesque fashion over the hair. It is extra- ordinary how femininity have decided to adopt the bow and ends of lace or ribbon, or, in some instances, flowers which fall either in the centre back or slightly to the left side down the hair to the shoulders. In some instances this mode is carried to an extreme, and loops and ends of black velvet ribbon not only fall on to the shoulders but extend to the waistline. rlt must, however, be admitted by all that there is some- thing rather cutre about this mode which will

prevent it from attaining to the highest point of favour in the estimation of the most cultured woman. The pretty hat sketched is of a simple design and particularly well suited for wear during the earlier hours of the day, provided the wearer resides in a fashionable suburb of a largo city, otherwise it is sufficiently smart to do duty at any hour of the day, except for the-most festive occasions. The straw is of a light fancy description, curved and bent to suit the face, and kept from drooping in an unbecoming and awkward manner by a skilfully arranged interthreatling of wire covered with silk to match exactly the tone of the straw. The trimming consists •ef shot pink foulard patterned with pink tastefully pnffed and swathed. One very pretty French hat I re- cently admired had its crew-n swathed with lace and silk, but what particularly attracted my attention was the fact that instead of tacking the trimming in place with a few careless stitches, pearl-headed and small jewelled piss were em- ployed, the result being quite sufficient firmness combined with a careless grace which was un- doubtegy the acme of perfection. Indeed, really skilful fingers should be able to place the trimmings of a smart hat in correctly with only the aid of a few pins, and the advantage of having those of an ornamental nature is obvious as very often one makes a greater success at the first attempt than when more time and pains are expended.

A pretty costume is here depicted -designed of black voile arranged over Chine silk trimmed and inserted with twine-coloured lace. The gown which formed the original of the sketch was one which had done good .simvioe during

the preceding months,' but with a little additionai trimming emerged into all the beauty of a really charming as well as useful toilette. The collar of the dress is of original design, which would look equally well on a loose blouse. The lace insertion, as well as forming the bordering of the collar, s _ _ _ . .

is employed for the chemiette witl its transparent collar, and for the sleeves. The skirt is also adorned with the lace both as an insertion and for a border, and as it is in every case easily detached to be cleaned ite merits are at once discernable.

I have been mach struce with the evolution of the underskirt or petticoat (as it used to be termed) which this season is so delightful a garment as to create a doubt as to concealing its beauties beneath the still more charming toilette which generally shrouds its charms. The pretty specimen sketched is particularly suited for summer wear, as it is made, en princesse, the skirt being continued npwards-in very much the same fashion as a Swiss belt, two small straps crossing the shoulders and so kefping the upper por- tion in place. The skirt is of greater length than usual, and SO can be worn nadir an-unlined muslin

• lace costume. It is best to have such a piece of dress made specially, as the ready-made articles will neither wear nor fit so well. Some girls make a dainty and rather fussy frill or flounce of muslin lace trimmed and inserted, which, indeed, to be correct should have a profusion of lace frills. This is attached to the underskirt by buttons and buttonholes so that it can be very quickly detached. II always advise anyone who seeks advice to buy a really good silk underskirt, as it is a good investment. If (as is often the case) it is unlined, either remedy this fault yourself or get it done for you, as a lining of sateen or (even muslin will make the skirt wear twice as long, and therefore more than repay the trouble and time expended on so doing. Some people now-a-days consider the lacey petticoat has fallen from its position by reason of common imitations, and have substituted embroidery in its place.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

We shall all Aare in the rejoicings in Holland over the ; ptobability that Queen Wiltelmina will be, in course of time completely restored to health. The life of the girl Sovereign is not only of political import, but she has always been a picturesque figure, which has appealed very strongly to our national temperament. This feeling bas teen intensified by the many misfortunes that have marked the early years of her married life, and we can all jo,n in the unalloyed hope that her future may be a. , ;bright and happy one, and that she may be spared to; r people for a full span of years. The Doke of Connaught, accompanied by a brilliant; suite, left for Madrid on Monday to attend the fetes in connection with the coming of age of the young King of Stain. The festivities 6xtemd over several days, and in some respects they are on a grander scale than will be witnessed at the Coronation next month. There ie no Court in Europe, where Royal formalities are more strictly observed than in Spain, and no fewer than fifty different uniforms had to he provided for the Kiug, to enable him to appear in orthodox diem at the various eeremonies. King Alfenso is new the youngest reign- ing Monarch in Europe, and though his physical de- velopment leaves much to be desired, he is well edu- cated, and is a thorough master of French, English, and German.

It is fortunate that all our dreams do not acme true oven though the picture presented to us is sometimes all that the •Leart could -desire. An old lady living at Croydon who dreamt, on more than one occasion, that the Queen had presented her withia chair, a shawl, and a Bible, has, hrwever, had her dream fulfilled in a way that must give her infinite satisfaction. The repetition of the dream worried the old lady so, that she wrote to the Queen about it, with the result that her Majesty sent a shave! and a Bible, Possibly a good 'many ether I people will dream of Royal gifts,but it will be too much to expect that they will all be forthcomian, as in the case of the old lady at .Croydon. The Twentiathilentury Club, which is shortly to be opened at Notting Hl Gate, in London, will make a practical experiment in providing a home on cracr rative principles for ethieated woman workers. The dlfficulte which the bachelor woman has in Ending house accom- modation, suitable to her earnings and social position Inas enormously increased in recent years in London and also in the large towns, since women have taken more generally to seek their own livelihood aid independence. The experiacce of the Twentieth Century Club win; therefore beareatcbed "rip great interest. The chargel for a separate bedroom • is to be from 10s 6d to 15s a' week, with use of " common rooms," asd for a further 103 6d per week breakfast and dinner will be provided.; A woman would require at least £lOO a year to live at the club, but, if it succeeds, there is little doubt that others will spring up, where the charges will be less. Weather prophets generally achieve their nctariety by predicting the most unseasonable and inauspicious conditions,'Aanst when many people affect that summer is at hand. The prophets have one and all scored a success this year, and those of us who had toolishiy acted as ifthe winter had _gone. have suffered a good :eat in the-bitter winds whicn have played havoc with our ideal notions of the merry month of May. The wive have taken heedful note of the old saw, " Ns'er east a clout till May be Out" and will wait awhile yet 'ne they stow away winter garments. In this operation,naplathalene—or as some people term it, carbon-aeither in lumps, ar powder—is indispensable. ;Furs, underclothing, garments of every description, should be carefully brushed, shaken, and fo:ded, the naphthalene being slipped in plentifully between the folds. Many women possessed of valuable furs send Ithean in the spring to their furriers, set o, for a small charge guard tha furs from moth, during the summer imonthe. ',Bat this procedure is, quite useecessary, if the process described is carried out, moreover, by keeping cee's furs at home. one is ready • for emergencies—a desirable state of affairs in this very variable climate of ours. 'Nothing is batter too for stowing away blankete, aidardowns, heavy winter curtains, and hangings, than naphthalene A pound of it can be obtained for a few pence, and the disagreeable odour can to easily and 'quickly got rid of, by canoeing theatticles to the air. The feminine hat-pin will aeon have to be put in the same category as the knife, or the revolver. When mis- used by violent wren, no more deadly or brutal weapon could be imagined, and cases continua to multi- ply in which very'serious mil indeed fatal injuries are inflicted with bat-pine. It is most desirable in the public interest, that magistrates and judges should punish finch offenders:in an exemplary manner. If only the hat-pin could he dispensed -with altogether There seems howeverdittle chance of any better idea for keeping headgear firmly on our heads, coming to light, andaslastimis too hopelessly dowdy to be considered for a mordent.

With a•graceful figure. and a well-drrased head, the simplest:ottrilettea look well. To spend a considerable portion of °nee dress allowance with the hair-dr:sect, and corset-maker, would therefore •seem to be a Wife, procedure. 1n the matter of cozies, the newest !aft on either aide, instead of at the 'back, tbeetraight fronts otillerbtain, and promise to ,remeinitr. favour. As regartie the coiffure the hair may be worn either high or low., and with or without a light fringe. am preferred, but it must be very softly dressed,no stiff crimping or waving being perrn;esible. Jewelled pins and combs,which keep the poufs and twist(' in place, are much in evidence,and ;.re particularly beautiful. The VOEUR for deep corn-coloured hats and tsques, ccmhincd wlth black, has reached the point when well- dressed women prefer a different style. That it would ecome " too popular" was anticipated, but it is nevertheless a matter for regret, as .this style of heed.' gear goes well with any toilette. At the, moment, the turban trque witli round high lartm, is being donned by cp-to-date women. This is generally trimmed with fsuit, such as grapes, apples, currants, plums, the whole e rection invariably rroviog rzceedirgly unbecoming. The practice of passing on bad servants by giving false characters, or concealing disagreeable truths, is one from which many houseb.slders suffer. A fresh effort is being mane to introduce legislation, on the sub- ject in Parliament, but, as a matter of fad, there is already a sufficient remedy against such reprehensible conduct. Unfortunately servants cannot be improved by Act of Parliament, and the law against wrongful tee- V menials, is seldom put into operation,perhans becaus,l householders have found it cheaper, and irlinitely less trouble to put up with the first loss and annoyance._

The Hon. Ethel Gerard.—A Coronation Debutante.

"Miss Ethel Gerard, the young daughter of Lord and Lady Gerard, says the "Home rotes,"' is one cf the many pre.ty girls who may claim the title of Coronation debutantes. Miss Gerard inherits her Leauty from her mother, and, like her, she is many- sided in her interests and hobbies. Lord and Lady Gerard are a great deal at Cowes during the season, and she is a first-rate and most enthusiastic yachts- woman. She is also a splendid rider to hounda,and in her love of sport she has her daughter's sympathy for Miss Gerard is probably never happier than when spending the hunting season in the neigh- bourhood of a famous pack. Lady Gerard in a woman on whom Fortune has smiled, and her ydung daughter is one of the most populargirls in London. Miss Gerard has a great love of art and beauty, and she is :considered (lite of the best dressed girls in society; her taste in manners sartorial is one of the many good things she has inherited from her mother, whose tall and graceful figure is always perfecrly gowned. THE
AN OLD SCORE,
BY ADELINE SERGEANT (Author of" The Lady Charlotte," ON)
PART 1.-CHAPTER t
" Yon were the woman F"
'Yes, it was I."

The man who spoke was flushed, appealing, eager: the woman beside him, although perfectly pale, showed no sign of emotion in her face. They were walking aide by side on a broad grassy road or track which ran into the very heart of the woodlands; on either side the trees raised their mighty arms so high that little of the blue sky could be seen between their fluttering yellow leaves. Yet the sunshine filtered down upon the bracken and the bramble bushes be- neath the boughs, and bars of light lay athwart the delicate shadows through which the man and woman trod. Olwen thought vaguely to herself that the play of light and shade symbolised the chances and changes of the life that she had led ; but Maurice Harding, at her side, was -far too busy with his own views and aspirations to be alive to symbols. He was a hard-headed, sceptical man by nature; and Olwen Dare was a fanciful woman in her way. They were both noticeable people in appearance. , Harding was above the middle height; he had broad shoulders, and a lithe, sinewy figure. His face was ugly—there was no denying the fact; the features were dark, rugged and stern, but the deeply set eyes were remarkable for their brilliance, and the droop- ing moustache hid some irascible lines about the mouth. There was energy, decision, determination in the face, but not much softness, and certainly no u-ealmess of any sort. One could well imagine that his fame as an explorer of a singularly daring naturt had been well deserved. Miss Dare was tall—for a woman—, and she was also beautiful. The ,perfect proportion of her limbs gave tier a grace of -movement which had been the first cause of Harding's attraction towards her: she walked, he said " like a savage queen," not like a modern, conventional, young lady of society. This speech might have prejudiced society against Miss Dare—for Harding's criticisms were respected—, had she not been already popular and rich. She might walk " like-a savage queen." as much as she pleased, and still be admired. As a matter of fact, her graceful walk and dignified carriage were truly admirable. For the rest she was rather pale, with a beautifully shaped oval face, dark waving hair, and grey eyes with long curry lashes. She had the ex- cellent gift of a sweet voice and a sweeter smile; and by dint of her many graces and beauties she hadtaken captive the heartof Maurice Harding, and brought him —a very slave—to her feet. And now, when the de- cisive moment had come, and he had poured out the story of his love, she calmly and coldly refused him, and told him why. They were walking in the park bZonging to a country house where they were• guests. People asked them together, as all the world expected daily to hear that they were engaged. It would surprise the world as much as it surprised Harding to know that she had refused him: for she had given him open and marked encouragement. And she was not a woman who dispensed her favours lightly. He had proposed, and, in refusing him she had added a few pregnant sentences of explanation that caused him to utter the words already recorded— " You were the woman ?" And she had answered, "Yes, it was L" "But I did not know you—l had no idea," he stammered.

"That was where the injustice of the thing came in," said Olwen calmly. 'You did not know me, you knew nothing about me, except that I was a young girl, living in the country, poor, untaught, not a match, as you considered, for your friend, and therefore to be branded as an adventuress. Oh, yes, I have seen the letter you wrote about me to Lionel Borzodaile, and a more uncalled for attack upon a girl's character and reputation I never imagined to myself. If we were not in polite society, and bound by the chains of convention, I should say—" She stopped suddenly, and seemed to consider. Harding, very white beneath his bronze, and biting his moustache furiously, turned to hear the end. "Go on," he said harshly. "We are not polite society,' you and I. You may be as free from con- vention aS I am, if you like. You would say what?" " I should say," she proceeded calmly, "that you had lied."
"Do you laaow what you are saying? Dc you know how you are insulting me ?" he broke out, in a hoarse. suffocated. voice.
"Perhaps you forget that you insulted me— onGe," she said, in passionless, level tones._

"Not purposely ! Not knowingly! I was de- ceived. 1 swear it, Olwen, on my life and soul I ...wear that I was told of a very different woman, and what I said of her was true enough, but it was never said of you." "Excuse me, I saw the letter. All the things you said Were spoken of Miss Durant. I was Mist Durant—l changed my name when money was left to me by my Godmother. Lionel had been spend- ing the summer in our village, you will remember, and I was a girl of nineteen teaching in the village school. We knew each other—we loved each other a little—perhaps; he asked me to be his wife. You know why I was not." "Good heavens! Who would have thought it Borrodaile must have been a weak fool—"

"Do not atom e a man who is dead," said Olwen quietly. "You were his guardian: he naturally attached some value to your opinion. When you wrote to,him, ordering him back to town, and in- forming him that you knew—knew, mind you, that I was an unprincipled little adventuress and worse. a woman of evil reputation, in fact ; it was natural that he should be startled."
"He showed you my letter? And you put up with such an insult ?"
" The insults were in the letter: his showing it to me was a detail. He was in great trouble over.it. I advised him at once to obey his guardian and go back to London—" " And he went !"

$‘ It is absurd for you to be indignant, Mr. Hard- ing. You know that he went, and. why. You know that you threatened him with all sorts of pains and penalties if he did not return to London immediately. :1 seconded your efforts to the best of my ability. I .told him to obey you, and to come back when—or if —be obtained your consent. He never came back." -" And you blame me for that ?" " Well, naturally. You kept him in town, did you 'not?''

_ "Tor. loved him ?—that boy ?" ."J loved him—as well as I knew how." " And you have never forgiven the man who separated you ?" She hesitated before replying, but spoke at last in a clear and resolute tone.

" The separation was hard to bear. It did not break my heart, but it gave me much pain. He never wrote to explain why he had abandoned ine, but I knew well enough that it was because of your advice—your opinion. And when I realised, after weeks and months of suspense and misery, that you had triumphed over me and got the poor boy under your thumb ?gain, then I said to myself—"
She paused again, but as he maCle an eager gee. ture, she resumed her speech. _ _

"'I said to myself that if ever I met the man who had shown himself capable of such cruelty to an 1171-•• offending girl, who had tried to blacken her reputa- tion in the eyes of the man she loved, ' and shown. neither :mercy nor justice in his anxiety that his ward should marry a wealthy woman—if I met that man, I should be glad if in any way I could make him suffer. It was unlikely that I should ever meet him; but you see, the unlikeliest things sometimes happen—and—now that I am a rich woman and Lionel Borrodaile is dead—we have met." " Then am I to understand that you deliberately ept yourself to attract me, with the intention of re- fusing me should I be so blind as to walk into your trap ?" She raised her eyebrows and glanced at him with a bitter smile. "Can you wonder at it? Have I injured you more thap you injured me? Yes,as soon as I knew who you were, I set myself to make you like me: hOped that you would fall in love with me, and give me the opportunity of refusing the man who once told his ward that a marriage with me would mean Social suicide."

Harding uttered a sound of mingled anger and despair, then walked on in silence for some minutes, his head hanging, his hands thrust deep into his pockets. When he spoke, it was in short, jerky sen- tences, which showed more clearly than elaborate periods would have done the keenness of his pain. "I was a brute, I know. And a fool too, it seems. It's useless to try to exculpate oneself, but at the time . . . I heard all the things—those things in the letter—about the woman who taught that school: I believe they were true. She was dismissed after- wards for misconduct. . . . But, of course, that's nothing to the point. I can only say that I regtet my action—l regretted it long ago when I taw Lionel's dorelopment. There's nothing more to be said but to beg your pardon—and go." Olwen turned her head away. This manner of treating the subject startled her. The man's humil- ity was utterly unexpected. She had looked for a etorra_of rage. a tempest of reproaches, and these
ltould

Itave-relievect-ter is Etrre, for her conscience was not altogether at rest when she thought of the way in which she had treated Maurice Harding; but it disconcerted her to be met with this acknowledge- ment of wrong-doing, this abasement of spirit, in the man upon whom she had tried to wreak her re- venge. She wished she could relent: she wished she could say something to atone for her past bitter- ness. But she had gone too far. It was hardly possible for her to take back what she had said. Besides, she had remembered her wrongs for seven years and more: she had acted on meeting Hard- ing, as she had always meant to act; and how could she stultify herself by owning to a softer mood P Still, the look of dumb misery on Harding's face troubled her. She wished she could speak of some other subject, so as to lead his mind away from the proposal of marriage that he had made; but she felt that she had neither strength nor courage enough to do so. She was almost relieved when he same to a sudden stop, and confronted her. "I won't afflict you with my presence any longer," he said, in his harshest voice. "I can but say I am sorry—and I'll leave the house to-night. I congratulate you, Miss Dare: you have had your revenge, and you. had a right to it. Fate does not always give us the chance of paying off an old score; but you are fortunate and have paid it in full—and with interest. I will wish you good-bye now. You are close to the garden-gate, so you will not need a guide any further. Good evening." "Oh, Mr. Harding, surely you will not go like this I—l—am sorry—" . _

" Sorry ? After attaining your end 89 complete- ly ? Oh, that is impossible," said Harding, smiling and raising his hat. And Olwen could say no more. But she did not forget the mute reproach of that pale face, with the sombre eyes and the frow-..i of pain upon the brow.

"Harding has been called away on business," the host explained that night at dinner. "A sudden telegram—something very important, I believe. I daresay Miss Dare can tell us what it is," and the Squire indulged in a chuckle which brought a flush of unwonted colour to Olwen's pale cheek. "I know nothing of Mr. Harding's affairs," she said so coldly that the Squire floundered into a sort of apology. "Of course not, my dear, Why should you? But as I saw you walking with him in the park just be- fore he was summoned away, I thought you might have heard what it was."

The Squire's w-ife lookeddaggers at him. "what an absurd idea to suppose that Mr. Harding would. talk business to a young lady '." she said lightly; but she did not do away with the uncomfortable impression that had been produced. Some of the guests glanced oddly at Miss Dare: it was felt that an explanation of Mr. Harding's departure ought to come from her. Everyone knew, or thought that he had been on .the brink of a proposal; and, of course, she meant to accept him or she would never have received his attentions 80 complacently. If it had been mere flirtation on her part, and she had refused him after all—why, then, Olwen Dare had behaved disgracefully and deserved the reprobation oi all well regulated minds.

But olwen gave no sign. She conversed with her neighbours in a particularly agreeable manner, and professed herself quite unable to give any reason for Mr. Harding's sudden departure. She hoped that she would escape without further questioning, but she was not to be let off quite so easily. Her hostess, a large, fair woman with a passion for match-making, followed her to her room.
"New, dear, do tell nie," she said, "whether Maurice Harding did not give you some clue as to why he was going 80 suddenly." " I am not in Mr. Harding's confidence," said Olwen, with a blush.

" Oh, that's all nonsense," said Lady Diana—she was an Earl's daughter, although she had married only a country squire, and she thought herself an adept in the art of advising young people about their love affairs. "We all know that he was desperate- ly in love with you—"

" Please donit say so, Lady Diana !" " But I will say so, child, because I know it for a fact," said the lady, settling herself in a big chintz covered chair, and holding out one foot towards the fire in the grate. "He told me 8011113 days ago how much he admired you, and I told him to go in and win, for I was sure he would be successful." ,
"I don't think you were quite justified in saying that to him."
" Oh, don't you, my lear ? You girls are very faddy sometimes. But you've shown us so plain- ly that you were as much in love with Harding as Harding was with you—"

Olwen started up, her face all in a blaze. "I have not have not !" she cried passionately. " I —I ?—sltow that I was in love P—l was not I was not—l could not show it when Suddenly she covered her face with her hands and burst into tears. " Oh, I don't know what I'm saying—l think lam mad!• Forgive me—" and then came a gasping sob.

Lady Diana sat still, and nodded her head con- tentedly. "Don't mind me, my dear," she said. " Have your cry out—lt will do you good. You've quarrelled, I suppose? Never mind, we'll soon have him back again, and you sball make it up and be all the better friends. There's nothing like a tiff or two before marriage: better before than after, ,I al- ways say." Olwen lifted up,alear-stainedface from her hands. "But you are miStaken, Lady Diana. lam not going to marry Mr. Harding." "What ! Do you mean to say he went away Without proposing ?" said Lady Diana, almost jumping out of her chair. " You ought not—l ought not—l redly think we. might drop the subject," said Olwen, trying for haughty voice, but failing miserably in the at- tempt. "Don't be foolish, child: tell me the truth. You know I was fond of your mother, Olwen; you should look upon me as your best friend and con- fide your troubles to me. Did he propose or not? For if not, I shall really tell Mark to ask him hl3 intentions."

"Oh, Lady Diana, what an awful thing to do !" said Olwen, drying her eyes, and pretending to laugh. "Well, if I must tell you—yes, he did ask me to be his wife, and I—" "Has he gone to London to buy the ring ?" asked Lady Diana breathlessly. " I refused him," said Olwen, in an abrupt tone. " Refused him?" "Yes, Lady Diana. I—l never thought A ac- cepting him." 6‘ What ?"
"1 have no wish to become the wife of Mr. Hard- ing." • "Then 7."—with an accent of horror—" what on earth have, you meant by encouraging him as you have done

Olwen was silent: she would have given the world to be' able to say at that moment that she had not encouraged him. But it would not have been true. She stood, holding her handkerchief in her small clenched hands and looking down at the fire, while Lady Diana continued her remarks. "My dear Oliven, I should have thought that you would know better. Don't you see what a marked thing it has been from the very beginning? The man fell hopelessly in love with you from the first moment he saw you; and what I cannot understand is that you seemed to fall in love too! Yes, indeed you did: I watched you, and I know the signs." "You must have been mistaken. I was—amusing. myself: that was all." "Very wrong indeed. You went quite too far in your amusement, my dear. I am affaid other people will call it a flirtation—carried, I must say, to the very verge of impropriety. I never should have allowed him to be so much with you if he had not spoken to me and told me how he admired you, and, of course, I thought that you reciprocated his feeling." "I do not know why you should have thought

"Because you showed every sign of it, my dear. And if you were not in earnest, you have be- haved very badly, Olwen, and I should never have thought that you were so cold-hearted." "You don't know me, it seems, Lady Diana." " No, I suppose not. lam very much disap- pointed. I had quite set my heart upon this mar- „ln g tow people Will talk Come, omen, are you sure that it isn't a lover's quarrel? shall I write to him to come back again ?' " Certainly not. I wish neither to see nor to hear of Mr. I Harding again." " Yet you're fond of him ?" 4' /am not—l bate him." "I'll leave you to sleep on it," said Lady Diana, rising and gathering up her skirts. "It's my be- lief that whether you know it or not, you're in love with the man, if not, you've behaved abominably, and must expect to hear yourself milled a flirt and a jilt and other ugly names. Good night, my dear, telegraph to Harding whenever you like." Olwen,turned away with a gesture of anger; but when Lady Diana had gone, she threw herself on the bed face downward, and cried her heart out—as- suring herself at intervals that she knew not why. Was it possible she loved Harding after all ? 11 so, her case was hard, for she had sent him away from her with words of scorn and anger, and he was not the man to sue for her love a second time.
(To be Concluded.)
SKETCHES AT EARL'S COURT.
moment, How could they do otherwise when everything has been arranged, and, ignorin; the showering :skies and chilly winds, the public are siamouring for admittance? For, whatever the

weather, you will always find visitors at Earl's Court, which is certainly the most popular resort in London during the summertime. And then there is really no reason why one ghould sit out- side and starve if one does not want to. Of course, the music is almost irresistible, but there are plenty of equally fascinating attractions indoors, where warmth can be obtained and influenza avoided. Although the great wheel, the great dragon, the lake, the water chute, and the switchback are still there, all their surroundings have so completely changed since 'last year that it appears as though Earl's Court has been transported across the Straits of Dover to Paris, and not Paris to Earl's Court. "Paris in London " is, as Mr. Imre Kiralfy intended it should be, something more than a name, and there is not the slightest doubt that this year's exhibition will be a gjeater success than ever.— At the Apollo Theatre on Saturday night a musical comedy was produced under the auspices of Mr. George Edwardes, and it promises to score a success for that rising young author and composer, Mr. Paul Rubens, despite some inexplicable booing on the first night. All it requires to make it first-class of its kind are a few lively dances, which can easily be added, and the reception accorded to Mr. Edwardes only showed how fickle and exacting a well-catered-for audience can be. Three Little .111ititls is the tale of, a trio of country parson's daughters who come up to town to serve in a fashionable tea-shop, ostensibly to relieve the paternal purse, but really to catch wealthy husbands, and their vagaries in search of matrimony are exceedingly amusing. Miss Edna May (with a tuneful love song) and Miss Hilda Moody (with the hit of the piece, "The Miller's Daughter") are two of the trio, and the third was to have been Miss Ada Reeve who was, however, too unwell to take up the part. Her place was filled by Miss Madge Crichton, who proved herself an excellent deputy, and made an instantaneons success. She showed more capability for acting than is usual in such pieces. Amongst the men, Mr .i G. P. Huntley stood out prominently with another inimitable sketch of male manners of a certain type.

Everything was very bright and gay at the Kempton Jubilee meeting, and the executive was extremely fortunate in its weather. The racing was well up to the mark, and the big race proved most interesting, although Royal George won easily all the way. He was followed home by, ,Wargrave and Revenue, with Santoi, last year's winner, running a very good horse and finishing just out of a place. The Jubilee Stakes now-a-days is probably the most popular of the Spring handicaps, and an enormous concourse of penons of all sorts
IN THE PADDOCK AT KEMPTON PARK: TEE SeDILEE HANDICAP : ,RQTAL GEOII(}E LED I;

assembled to see it run, induding the King who struck everybody as looking extremely well and happy, as he strolled about the members' en- closure practically unattended in democratically regal fashion. All the prominent people in the racing world were prez.ent, and one of the chief topics of conversation was the health of Captain Machell, who died the following day. Certainly there was no better known figure on the race-course up to two years ago than the Captain, and no^Turf history of the last thirty or forty years could be written without being inextricably interwoven with his career, the horses he has owned, the horses he has managed, and the now prominent owners he has "god-fathered " on the, Turf. He first came into prominence over Hermit's historical and sensational Derby, when Mr. Henry Chaplin broke his successful rival in love, the late Marquess of Hastings, physically and financially in a heavy betting duel. Captain Machell managed Hermit, and netted a big win, since when he has always been to the front, having won for himself, apart from other people, over five hundred races and £lOO,OOO in stakes. Two years ago he broke down in health, and now the race-course can know him no more.

div.head: MARTINIQUE CATASTROPHE:
div.p: THE MARTINIQUE CATASTROPHE:
ST. PIERRE, THE CITY DESTROYED BY THF. I. PP lON 07 MOIIN l' PELEE.

Were it not that there is a suggestion of irrever- Wee in, the thought, one might well say that, by some mighty upheaval in the far-away past, the West Indian Islands had been thrust through the shimmering plain of the sunny Caribbean to be the sport of Nature. In a generous mood she bestowed her favours upon them with a lavish hand, and for the most part she continues to smile upon her tiny children fondly. 'But from time to time a frown disfigures the face of the fickle mother, and then in her anger she lashes them with a fury that knows no restraint. With a breath she will wither whole islands, dealing death and desolation everywhere. Then the terrible Spasm will pass away as suddenly as it appeared, and once more she, will bestow caresses upon her trembling offspring, reassuring the dwellers on the islands a little perhaps, but never winning their- full confidence, for well they know her uncertain temper, and how liable it is to break forth at any moment and sweep them from the face of the earth. Hitherto, however, the people in the West Indies have chiefly dreaded the devastating hurricane, with scarcelY a thought for another and a more awe-inspiring danger at their very doors. With the exception of Barbados, which is of coral formation, most of the islands forming the archipelago are of volcanic origin • in reality, a chain of mountain summits that Lave been raised by the internal expansive forces of the earth from the depths of the ocean. Almost all the islands have extinct or partially extinct craters, which, although some are in a modified form of activity have always been regarded as safe until the appalling catastrophe tat Martinique has proved the contrary to be the case. It is almost impossible for the human mind, even with the aid of a vivid imagination, to fully realise the awful nature of the disaster which has befallen the • flourishing French Colony, and in a lesser degree the neighbouring British colony of St. Vincent. The world's history fortunately records few such

overwhelming calamities. Indeed, the doom of St. Pierre can only be compared to the destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum more than eighteen hundred years ago, the earthquakes that destroyed Lisbon in 1531 and in 1755, and the eruption of Krakatoa, in the Sunda Straits in 1883. The latter disaster, in which it is estimated that forty 1 thousand people perished, is still fresh in our memories, but we were not so thoroughly and promptly posted up in all the harrowing details as we have been in the case of the West Indian horror, and, moreover, it did not touch us so nearly. By this stupendous tragedy the whole civilized world has been dazed, as it were, with a sudden and terrible s ock, and since the dreadful tidings came over the cable the fate of that stricken city has dined our hearts with sorrow and awe. To the survivors—alas that there should be so few !—we can send succour and sympathy, but the thousands who lie buried • beneath that lake of lava we can but mourn. As will be seen from our illustration St. Pierre was a picturesque city. For a West Indian town it was unusually well built, there being fewer wooden structures, and more stone houses, many of which had tiled roofs, giving the place a very pretty appearance when seen from the bay. The city lay at the entrance to a valley, and the out- skirts were almost on the lower slopes of Mount Pelee, which dominates the whole region. St. Pierre was the chief commercial centre of Martinique,.although Fort de France is the capital of the island. The amount of shipping in the harbour at the time of the eruption would pro- bably not be very large, and as the tonnage of the vessels using the port, or, at any rate, making any lengthy stay there, is never very great, the loss of life and property in the bay is as nothing compared to the havoc wrought ashore. Mount Pelee is 4,430 feet high, and had been quiescent for so } many years that it was believed to be quite I. extinct.

For the first time since the proud title was cony ferred upon him by the King, the Prince of Wales, accompanied by the Princess, visited the Princi- pality last week, and loyal little Wales rose nobly to the occasion and gave the HeilApparent a hearty Welsh welcome. The principal event during the Prince's visit was his installation at University College, Bangor, as Chancellor of ths
'Y COLLEGE, B.
WHERE THE PRINCE OF WALES WAS INSTALLED CHANCELLOR OF THE WELSH UNIVERSITY.

University' of Wales, in succession to his illustrious father, and the scene in the magnificent building where the ceremony was enacted was one which will live long in the memories of those who were privileged ,to witness it. The University of Wales consists of four colleges —St. David's, Lampeter, University College, Aberystwyth, University College of North Wales, Bangor, and University College of South Wales, Cardiff. It was founded by Royal Charter in 1893, and has power to grant the degrees of bachelor, master and doctor in the various facul- ties. Moreover, the degrees are open to women on exactly the same conditions as the men. The establishment of the Welsh University is the crowning point of the great Movement among the • Welsh people during the past fifty years for greater educational facilities available to them in their own country, and it is a monument of national enthusiasm for education which must not be measured by its material importance. One of the most Etriking features about the estab- lishment a the University is the practical interest manifested in the movement for its foun- dation by the middle and lower classes, a large proportion of the whole amount contributed being derived from a house-to-house canvass of the rural parts of Wales. The Prince as was his Majesty the King, may well be proud of his Chancellorship, and the whole country is proud of the University. The cuckoo and the nightingale do not wait for propitious weather when tne season comes round for them to pay us a flying visit, and, imitating their example, Mr Imre Kiralfy and his colleagues open their exhibition at Earl's Court at the begin- ning of May. however impossible al fresco enter- tainment of the kind they provide may be at the

--••- A ranketing of the Committee of the Northern Rugby League was held in Manchester on Tueeirty night, Mr J Clifford (Huddersfield) presiding. The question of the proposed extension of the League was under considera- tion and it was decided that if the number of applies- tions for admission warrant it the League should be extended at the proper time. It was, however, resolved that no application for admission he entertained except throughlthe medium of the new Second League, and it was further resolved to advertise for entries for that body. Messrs Citfford (Huddersfield), We!matey (Sal- ford), end Platt (Oldham) were appointed a sub-com- mittee to draw up rules for the Second Lray,fue. The following players were put on the registers of the Warritietott Club .—Ernest Breaker (Bowsey) and W Hind (Trinity). _ - Funeral of the Late Mr. William Cawley. The remains of the late Mr William Cawley, of Rowton, near Chester, who was a director of the firm of Messrs Arthur Waring and Company, tan- ners, Winwiek-strePt, Warrington, were interred at the Parish Church of Coddington. on Monday afternoon. After a short service at Brook Lodge, the late residence of the deceased, the funeral cor-- tege left for Coddington at half-pit twelve. In the first carriage were :—Mr John Cawley (brother) and his daughter, and two nieces (daughters of the late Mr Thomas Cawley) ; in the stcond, Mr Arthur and Mr Robert Cawley (nephewe),and Mr and Miss Hughes (brother-in-law and sister-in-law) ; in the third. the Rev L Garnett (rector of Cbriatleton), Mr John Roberts (WarrinZon) and Mr R Sal- mon, Rowton (trusteea); and in the fourth, Mr F A. Jowett (Liverpool), Mr T Butler, Mr J II Salmon and Mr Charles Higginbottom (Warrington) repre- senting Messrs Arthur Waring end Company, Limited) ; Dr Roberts (deceased's medical attend- ant) also attended, and several private carriages joined the cortege. At the church were Messrs Richard Brassey, Richard Coopar, Thorns s Cawley (Tarporley), George Penk, T Spencer Handley, T Walker (Russia Hall), R Mullach, It P Whalley and John Johnson. div.head: rhe Observance of Ascension Day.
div.p: rhe Observance of Ascension Day.

Preaching at St Paul's Church on Sunday evening, the Rev Morley Stevenson, the Principal of the Training College, alluded to the forthcoming coronation of the Ring and to Ascension Day. The latter was not, as Christmas Day was, a general holiday, and it was not, therefore, within the possibility of many people giving it that observance which their inmost feelings would Prompt them to give it. It was, however, vary much to be regretted that a day likg that, which had such a significance of meaning for all who were followers of Jesus Christ, and subjects of the King of kings, should have been pushed backwards, so to speak, into com- parative obscurity compared with the other great festi- vals, as the Ascension witnessed the coinpletion of a wonderful chain of events. Christmas Day heralded His birth, then they Passed through the sad times of His auffering and death; Easter Day chronicled His re,..,urrec• Lion, but Ascension Day put the crowning stone, as it were, upon the edifice, and so His work on earth was completed, and the redemption of mankind was won and death overcome. -

div.head: Returned Ambulance Men. Presentation of war Medals at Narrington. – –
div.p: Returned Ambulance Men. Presentation of war Medals at Narrington. - -

An interesting,and in so nre respects unique f anC- tion,took place at the Warrington Gymnasium on Thursday last week, when the Mayoress (Mrs J Charlton Parr) presented South African war medals to local ambulance men who have served at the front. This is the Bre!: occasion on which war machete have been presented at W arrineton, and considerable interest centred in the event. There was a good muster of members of the ambulance corps unaer the direc- tion of the superintendent (Captain Waring). The other officers present were :—First officer II T , Williams; second officer T.l Hulse; third officer Frederick Taylor, and Superintendent Baldry, The Mayor ( ir J Charlton Parr), presided over toe pro- ceedings, being accempanied by the Mayoress and the Misoes Parr. The attendance included Alder- Menke, Alderman Hutchinson, Colonel Ridgway, Councillors Smethurst. Bennett, and A Jolley. At the outset Captain Waring read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr R Pierpoint, Ml'., the ' Rector (Rev Canon Willis) and Admiral Jones Parry. Tee MAYOB then delivered a speech. He said that as Mayor of Werringten, and as one who had always taken a very deep interest in the ambulance movement, he felt it was a elle isure and a orivilego ta be called upon to preside and to assist toe Mayoress in that vein, inter- esting function-3 funczion which they all recognized as paying honour Co those to whom bonou'r was due and richly deserved. (Applause). He noticed, to begin with, the t that wa the first occasion upon which South African war medals had wen presented in Warrington. In the case of volunteers he was informed that they had been presented in Liverpool and Manchester, but that was the first time that the presentetion had taken plice at Warrington and he felt sere it would be grati- fying to the recipients to receive this reward in their native town, in the midst of their blends and kinsfolk, at the hands of alady who had the honour of represent- ing a moiety of the Mayoralty, and perheps he might be allowed to say the better half of the borough of Warring- ton. (Laughter.) The Mayor then went on to quote from a neeneoranduin which he said had been supplied to him by the boa secretary. The numb rof members of the corps who had eerved iii Seeth Africa was the very hand- some figure of twenty-two. Two of these 'were prevented from going out as ambulance men by being called upon as fighters, and one of them was badly wounded at Spion Rep. Ile (the Mayor) was rejoiced to hear from Captain Waring that that member was with them teat evening as he (Mr Parr) hoped recovered from that very dangerous wound. Eight of the twenty-two men were aill serving in South Africa, two, ho regretted t 2437', would return no more, and twelve had returned to receive the thanks of their grateful country. Two of those still serving cc:re doing so for the secold time, showing that at all events their ardour had not cooled, and their petrotisne had not grown less. 'two of the m3e, who snved in the Duke of Portland's hoepital, were presented with their medals by the CotnrnAnder-in-Cnief at Welbeck Ahbey, and one was to receive his at the hands of the Kieg. 'MN showe I the deep interest th t the King took in the movement and that he eves anotlous to promote it by every means in his pnwer. It might be interesting to receenize the growth of that corps since its formation in 1897. At that time the mcnabere in uniform were four officter4, three sergeants, an‘i twenty-nine rank and file, whilst at the present time there were five offioers, five sergeants, and forty-four rank and file, making an increase of eighteen. Tais be thought for the town of Warrington was not only a creditab'e but a very handsome number to teen- , tribute to that most useful institution. Ihe number of men holding the S;, John medallion was fifty and the number holding nursing c,n* ificates was forty. The number of service men supplied by the St John Ambi- ence Brigade throne,* et the country was2,ooo (Applause.) In conclusion the Mayor instanced the interest shown in the order by the late Queen Victoria and the Primo:: of Walee.The King also toek a very deep intereet in the movement and was anxious to premote it by every means in his power. The King had now been ' graciously pleased to accept the office of patron of the Brier,,ade, and had beee succeeded in the office of Grand Prior by his Royal Higeness the Prince of Wales. Titus they hal three generations of sovereigns, in prospect and past, all interested in the noble work. (Applause.) Tie &dewiness then gracefully performed the cere- mony of presenting the medals, the foil swing being the names of those who were entitled to them :
Suvrnumerary Officer EI T Williams 99 _ _
Privates S. • J Di inelo w _
~ G Kelly 9 9
Et Galloway J Maddock I.

W Johnson Unfortunately Private J Maddock succumbed to disease at Mal, king, and it was a touching incident , when the Mayoress pinned the medal on the breast of his little eon. Supernumerary officer J G Buckley and Private W Johnson are still serving in South Africa. Mr Bucicley's son received his father's medal, and Cap- tain Waring retained one hr Private Johnsoo. Having presented the medals the Mayoress handed re- examination certificates to the followiag members of the Corps :—John A Forshaw9 Joseph Lawless, Benjamin Green, James Tomlinson, George Garrett, Joseph Lowe, John Mahon, William E James, Samuel Pearson,Charlss Jones, John Wiltiam Gray, Thomas R Ashworth (all passed first re-examination) ; John Wilding, Fred C Bate, James Lee (passed final re-examination). Prizes for maxiraum attendance at drills were presented to Sergeants Newnes and Banning; and Privates Kirby, Dimelow, Tomlinson, Lee and Sayers. Private Tomlin- son also received a special prize, consisting of an eleotro plated butter dish, for attendance au the football field in uniform. Captain WARING proposed a vete of thanks to the Mayor and Mayoress and referred to several interesting facts in connection with the corps. Ile said that their team lost by only three points their chance of compet- ing in London for the Dewar shield. The Central Station team, nearly all members of that corps, brought back the silver shield from Widnes to Warrington again. Captain Waring referred to the assistance which had been re- ceived from the Crosfield family. There would be no Warrington corps, in uniform to-day had it not been for Captain Crosfield and the Crosfield family. The late Mr John Crosfield presided when the corps was first formed. The Gymnasium Committee had always shown them the greatest courtesy and kindness. The Mayor,Mr J Charl- ton Parr, had always willingly lent the corps a helping hand, and had assisted financially every member that they had sent out to South Africa. Colonel RIDGWAY seconded and said he was pleased to hear of what Captain Crosfield had done for the Corps. El 3 was reminded that Captain Crosfiald was now on the sea, hiving sailed with his company of Im- perial Yeomanry once more to do his duty for his country. They all wished him " God-spend" and a safe return. The vote of thanks Was accorded with cheers and the Mayon having responded the proceedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem.

BALLOON DISASTER IN PARIS. —The ascent of the balloon Pax at Paris on Moaday resulted in the death of the owner, M. Severo,and, an engineer named Sachet, who wag in the employ of the firm who made the motors for the airship. M. Severe's intention was to sail to I sy, but as a preliminary he put the machine through a cerise of evolutions for at least twenty minutes in the aerostatic park at Vaugirard. Some stoppages occurred at the outset, but the balloon at length moved steadily away in the desired direetioa. I Soon a flame was seen, followed by an explosion, and the airship dropped to the ground from an altitude of about 150 yards. The engineer Sachet was burned in a r shocking manner, and the body of M. Severe, who fell lon his feet, was horribly mutilated. Another engineer I was to have taken part in the ascent, but he had to be left behind fa the last moment, as he would have made r the machine to heavy. M. Severo's wife and. family I witnessed the disaster.

div.head: NATIONAL FOOD SUPPLY.
div.p: THE NATIONAL FOOD SUPPLY.

The Council eadorsad the teLowing resolution drawn up by the London Trades and Labour Couacil :—That this Trades Council is of opinion that should this country become involved in a European war, bread would rapidly rise to famine price?. Such a state of ' affairs, if nothing be done beforehand to guard against it, will prove a source of the very gravest national danger. The immediate Insult of bread riv,ing to such famine prices will be the very createst possible distress and misery and VIIIIi- Arvati3n amongst the working classes. Our reasons for this opinion are—(l) The changed indus- trial conditions of the present day, and the vast poverty-stricken masses congered in our great cities. (2) There are nearly 7,000,000 p ople to-day liviog in poverty so dire that they can hardly eke out a tare sub- sist(nee, even at present pricE,w. They will not be able to pay famine prices. (3) The disruption of trade which must accompany a European war will throw a further very large number, how large cv nnot be fore- ' seen, out of work—wageless ; they will not he able to purchase food. (II) It is not necessary for us to point out that the prolongation of the war means the starvaton of the poor and not the rich, and as week by week the pinch of hunger is felt more and more, we will not picture the consequences, which can- not fall Coon of a national calamity. We,ttierefore,call upon the Government to institute an inquiry Lto the present perilous position of this country in regard to its food supply in consequence of ear dependence upon foreign countries, and t a take measures to remedy this dangerous state of affairs.

Mr GREALEY proposed that it was desirable to have a resident factory inspector. H 4 pointed out that breaches of the law frequent'y occurred because there was no inspector living, ia the town. The SECRETARY said he was in communication with the Chief Inspector of :the Manchester district, and it Was desirable that this matter should be adjourned until ha badifurther information. They wou'd not be in a position to make an application to the Rome Office until they could show by definite information that it was necessary to have a resident in Teeter. Ere had ascertained that the Chief Inspector had four assistants and the factories, including laundrie.. in the district numbered 3,572 and the workehops 5,429, The total number of accidents reported during tho year 1900 wa 4,641, but in his (Mr Stott's) opinion it was certain that three times that nuceb7r occurred and were net report d. , It was decided to adjourn the further consideration of , the matter until the next meeting.
THE RECENT ACTION AGAINST A TRADE UNION. THE CASE FROM THE SOCIETY'S POINT OF VIEW.

At the close of the ordinary business Mr Buckley, the delegate of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners, referred to the recent action brought against the society at Manchester Assizes. He said teat up to new only one side of the question had been taken: The society had never taken the trouble to defsed them- selves really, but an address had now hese issued from the general office by their general secretary and with the permission of the Council he would like to read it as that the members would know the real facts of the case and hew the society steed in the matter. Mr FLANNERY thought that as it was getting late the matter might be postponed until the next meeting. Mr FLINSTON said they might want to di cuss, it and he also thought it advisable to adjourn the matter. Mr BUCKLEY said it was net a question for discussion. it was simply a matter of defending the society. Up to now they had made no defence. The !Council decided to hear the report and Mr Buckley proceeded te read it as follows :—This action has been described by newspaper writers in a variety of catchy headlines, such as " trade union tyranny," the tactics ef trade unions," etc, but the actual cirenea- stances which led up to these pioeeediags being breught against the society are of the ordinary character. A mixed body, composed of unionists and non-uniodits determined to come out on strike, in the hope that by this means their employers might be induced to con- cede a slightly increased remuneration for their laboor. A non-union man has made ne attempt to provide ways and means of keeping himself and fe milt- whilst out o- empleyment,bence his humiliating and dep-ndeit wind i tion. But,through his spectacles he regards himself as a benefactor to his fellows, a veritable hero,saerificing his employment for the benefit of union men and closing his eyes to the fact that, if successful, he will derive pre- cisely the same advantages as they. He prefers his adherence to the principles of trade unionism, and says he has always stood up for the maintenance of the privileges and rights of his trade. He IS pitied and taken on the backs of the union men, who carry him about for six or eight weeks, at a cost of 145 per week out of their hcal funds. T show that his prefessices are cot mete words he actually pays 25 61 pr mosal money out of one of his weekly in- stalments given him by society men and promises to complete the transaction as soon as he starts work. To hasten on this day the union men find him employment, pay his fare to the job, and from that moment his goed resolves vanish into thin air, and no more is heard of him for many months. One fine day be returns to the town, not to keep his promise by joining the union, but to g,i) straight into the one black shop established in their midst, and had be remained there he would have been in co egessial com- pany, but, unfortunately, his next move is into another where he is thrown among Iroise men. Ills pres- ence is resented and again he renews his professions cf unionist principles and expresses a desire to he pr-- posed again as a member, hut having regard to his general ungrateful behaviour in the pest, he is refused admission. The ehjaction to asseciato Eitb him is strongly felt by the union men in the shop where he is working, and unless something is done in the matter they will leave the employment, and te avoid this a de- putation is appeinted by the branch or branch C9Ol- - to see the manager and for:man in order to ascertain whose SPrVICES are most valuable to him:eud he (the manager) elects to discharge the objectionable man rather than lose the remainder. Leal proceedings are at *nee instituted against the society and £5OO damages claimed on his behalf, a fifth of wheh is awarded him Itiy a jury. There was no dificuesion on the matter. div.head: DEATH OF MR. WALTER ASHTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. WALTER ASHTON.

Former Warrington Bank Manager. Many Warrington people will regret to hear of the death of Mr Walter Ashton, formerly manager of the Warrington Branch of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, Limited, which teak place at Droitwich on Sunday. The deceased gentleman, who was 82 years of age, had been staying for some little time at the Droitwich Hotel. 1e was tnaoager of' tLie Warrington Dis- trict Bank for many years, holding the position from the time of the erection of the present premises, and he left Warrington about 28 years ago to become manager of the Sheffi-dd Waterworks. As is customary with bank officials he did not identify himself with the public affairs of War- rington, but was prominently connected with ' Wycliffe Church, the printed year books of which : show that he:was a member from 1838 to 18M. The Rev John Yonge. to whom we are indebted for this information, believes his connection with the church dates as far back as 1863, His wife, who was a daughter of the Rev Robert Halley, D. D., at one time minister of the Cevendishestreet Chapel, Manchester, was buried here seven years ago. From Sheffield the late Mr Ashton went to Haydock in the service of Messrs Richard Evans and Company. He retired from business s veral ysars ago, and lived at Southpo for aria tints, if -,ervar -Is going to London. He was highly esteemed by those who remember himhere, aryl tne newt of his death will , he received with regret. THE FUNERAL. !

_ The funeral took place at the Warrington Ceme- tery on, Wednesday afternom the offgaiinz minis- ter beingthe Kis, John Tonga. The mourners were ' Mr Arthur Ashton, barristes London an 1 Mr Her- bert Ashton, Liverpool (son), Mr R A Hampson (son-in-law), the Rev John Cheatham. Manchester, Mr R G Henshall (representing the Bsuk), Alder: man Roberts, Alderman Monks, Mr David Garnett Mr Matthew Knowles, rind Mr T Ashley. Floral tributes were sent hi the deceased gentle rr an's four children, Mr A Ashton, Mr Fl Ashton, Mrs Hatton and Mrs Rampeon, and Mr William long. The coffin bore the inscription:—" Walter Ashton, died May 11th, 1902, aged 82 years."

div.head: MAY 16th 1902
div.p: MAY 16th 1902
BACK TO PROTECTION

Tim CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER has imposed two new taxes, both of which have encountered considerable opposition. There was, first, a tax of one penny on CHEQUES AND cheques. It was an irritating CORN. little tax, which would have • impoverished nobody,. though it might have disorganised the business of banking and annoyed some large firms which prefer to pay the wages of their employees in paper rather than in cash. But the bankers and the large employers happen to have the ear of the Government. The tax has been withdrawn. The rather ignominioUs ,announcement was made just a few minutes after Mr. TOULMIN had taken his sat for Bury. A typical industrial town had sent him to the House to protest against the tax. A meeting in Hyde Park had endorsed the verdict of Lancashire. But the Bread Tax is a tax on the food of the very poor. It struck at no powerful

interest. The City was quite unconcerned,and the great banks sent no deputations. And so the tax remains. Yet there was in the minority against it one vote which outweighed all those which had been cast for it, for it happened to be the only vote which came direct from the people. The Government's majority was elected on a totally different issue. There was no hint dropped in the hurried trickery of the Khaki Election that Pro- tection was to be re-enforced and the Corn Laws revived. The Government has absolutely no man- date for what it is doing. On the other hand, there is no mistaking the meaning;of the Bury bye- election. Tee town has voted stea•lily Unionist for seventeen years. Eighteen months ago it gave its Conservative member a majority of over eight hundred. That majority has melted away,and in its place is:a Liberal plurality of over four hundred. The Tax was the one issue debated. All the old half-forgotten controversies about the big loaf and the little loaf were revived. The old cause, which first triumphed in Lancashire under the leadership Qf Costonii and Barour, proved that it had lost none of its vitality. Free-Trade may be a fly- blown phylactery,but it is an adornment which the Lancashire working-man is not ashamed to wear.

THE Tory defence of this tax on the food of the very poor consists in a series of contradictory evasions. On Budget night the CHANCELLOR declared that the poor would THE FOOD oF not pay it because the price THE POOR. of bread would not rise. Now that the price of bread has in fact risen, he argues that the poor ought to pay, adding at the same time that they will not feel it. He begins, however, by ignoring the wastefulness of such a tax. To raise a sum of 21 millions for the EXCHEQUER it mulcts the con- sumer of something over twice that sum For While only foreign corn and flour pays the tax, the holne-grown and home-milled article also rises in price. Then while the tax only imposes a duty equivalent to about half a fathing on the quartern loaf the baker raises his price by a halfpenny. In this way the poor man is robbsd even of the poor satisfaction that he is helping his country. The ma) )r part of what he i.;ays goes not to the ExcIIEQUER, but to the interests which the tax seeks to protect—the farmer, his landlord, the miller, and the retailer. A more wasteful tax could hardly be devised. The argument that the poor will not suffer pro- ceeds on a complete misunderstanding of facts. The middle classes will not feel the burden, and to the prosperous artisan it is not perhaps a very serious matter. But what of the agricultural labourer whose wages aro a bare twelve shillings a week ? To him the tax means at least a loss of sixpence a week. Sir HENRY FOWLER read a pathetic letter, which he had received from a labourer's wife :

We are asked to pay more for everything since the war began, oven for a reel of cotton or coals, and aiso on meat and other articles. I have eight children, and I know all about what sht.rt commons on Ils, a week m,a9, and I know there are many

who are worse off than I am. She winds up by explaining that to her the bread tax means that the one piece of meat which the family were able to afford on Sunday is gone. This is not an isolated case. In Est London the exhaustive statistics of Mr. CHARLES BOOTH show that out of a popula- tion of 904,000 some 111,000 are in chronic and severe want, 75,000 are generally ill-fed, and 129,000 are occasionally ill-fed, To these 315,000

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup
skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: persons the Bread Tax means a further burden of hunger and misery. In every provincial town those conditions are repeated more or less exactly. But there are even lower depths of poverty than this. There are thousands of hovels in the West of Ireland where a loaf of braad is a luxury almost as rare as a piece of beef to an English labourer's family. A tax like this has no immediate results, and its slow effects may long pass unnoticed. But in the long run it can only make want more chronic and more pressing, prosperity less continuous and assured. And we need only add that it was flagrantly unnecessary. Sir WILLTAM HARCOURT and Sir HENRY FOWLER had little difficulty in prov- ing that the money could have been raised from tobacco or beer, or from both. A democratic Chancellor would have graduated the income tax or turned his attention to ground values or publicans' licenses.

THERE is an impression abroad that this tax on bread is a temporary war tax. It is nothing of the kind, and the CHANCELLOR has explained quite frankly that when the war COME TO comes to an end the Income STAY. Tax will be lowered before

the Bread Tax is removed. It is the fruit of an agitation which began long beiore the war started, " to broaden the basis of taxa- tion." It is the result of a tendency which has grown over since 1895 towards prodigal expendi- ture. While the country imagines that its present burdens are due to the war, the real fact is that by doles and extravagance and bloated armaments our permanent national expenditure has risen by leaps and bounds. In 1895 it stood at 101 millions. Next year, if the war ends this month, it cannot be less than 145 millions—adopting the calculation of Lord WELBY, than whom there is no higher authority on finance. Somehow this great burden has to be met. Moreover, the leaning to Protection is part of the movement for Imperial Federation which IMr. CHAMBE aLA.IN inaugurated in 1896 with a proposal for an Imperial Customs Union, which is to tax all foreign produce, while it admits the ex- ports of the Colonies free. That means a tax not only on corn, but on meat and sugar as well. Against that proposal a rigid maintenance of Free-Trade was our only bulwark. If once the country becomes accustomed to protective taxes on food, it is inevitable that the Colonies will de- mand their share of the benefit.

The bye-election at Bury has done much to shatter the prestige of this Government. This typical industrial town has voted steadily Union- ist since 1895. Only eighteen months ago Mr Toulmin was defeated by over 800 votes. Since then no less than 1,200 electors have changed sides, and the Liberal minority becomes a majority of over 400. A Alamo so amazing can be due to no local accident. The constituencies are weary of an epoch of adventure and reaction, and the trick which won a general election no longer serves. In the country at large the Goveranaent had in October, 1900, a majority of one man in nine. At Bury one man in eight has changed sides. And there is no reason to suppose that this movement of opinion is confined to Lancashire. There is no doubt about Its cause. The Education Bill played its part and turned the votes of some Nonconformists. The revival of coercion kept the Irishmen loyal to the party of progress and conciliation, though as good Catholics they had every temptation to vote for the endowment of sectarian schools. But it was the Bread Tax which rallied the working classes to the Liberal standard, and induced the labour organisations to work earnestly for the very candi- date whom they had declined to support in 1900. The tradition of Free-Trade is not yot dead in the country, and a tax on the food of the very poor is still as unpopular as it was in the generation of Cobden and Bright. The Government sought no mandate in 1900 for any single item of its exten- sive programme of domestic reaction. Nothing was heard during the general election about the revival of the Corn Laws, the resuscitation of coercion, or the destruction of School Boards. For these schemes the Government had no vestige of authority. The Bury poll proves how little the co•intry approves them even in a stronghold of Unionism.

The National Liberal Federation could have met under no better auspices. The Government has succeeded in bring unity to the Liberal party. The "Liberal League," no doubt, is still in being, and its ample funds enable it to introduce confusion by buying the allegiance of certain Li'oeral agents. But it has no power which a cheque cannot buy, and even its chieftains are beginning to work once more with their old colleagues. Mr Asquith is as sound as Mr Bry-Je on the Education question, and Sir Henry Fowler as loyal to Free-Trade as Sir William Harzourt. Nor do any practical ques- tions divide the party on the South African issue, Mr Asquith spoke as strongly as Mr Morley on the Cartwright case, the typical instance of thesabuses of martial law. There is no dispute about the folly of unconditional surrender. Amnesty, compensation, and self-government are the watchword of the whole party practically of the whole country. One issue only divides the dissentients from the main body of Liberal opinion—the question of Home Rule. The Liberal Lsage has issued a manifesto on this ques- tion which seems to mark the absolute abandon- ment of all Mr Gladstone's principles in this matter. It was an odd moment to choose. The revival of coercion proves once more that self- government is the only alternative to repression. Simultaneously the two Premiers of Canada and Australia, Sir W Laurier and Mr Barton, have added their testimony to that of the late Mr Rhodes on behalf of Home Rule from an Imperial standpoint. Under the lead of Mr T W Russell, the Unionist North of Ireland is coming into line with the Catholic South. Only the Liberal League moves backwards. Luckily, the Bristol meeting has reaffirmed the true Liberal doctrine by passing a resolution in favour of the creation in Ireland of a body with power to legislate on all Irish ques- tions.

The Education debate was valuable not only for the searching criticisms which came from both sides of the House, but also for such of the de- fences of the Bill as were candid. Lord Hugh Cecil had the merit of exposing the real motives of the Clerical party, which alone gives its unreserved support to the Government's measure. In his view a " Voluntary " School is a building "with two doors." Into one of them the children are forced by law. The second leads from the school to the church. A " clerical " school is, therefore, not merely a place where dogma is taught, but a place whose whole reason for existence is the maintenance of a clerical atmosphere. That is the extreme Anglican, as it is also the Roman Catholic ideal. It is a view to be combated only when it is accompanied by a demand that such schools shall be maintained at expense. Under the present Bill, PcaoY-oeprated committees, its " control" by twphrieOuh xryait,tseits one-third minority of public representa- tives on sectarian committees, there is nothing to prevent the realisation of Lord Hugh Cecil's ideal. While such an ideal persists, thera can be no slackening in the counter-demand that every school which is maiatained froth the rates shall be controlled not partially, but absolutely, in every detail of its general management ,and its secular instruction.
