For the next few days the public mind will lightly turn to thoughts of how to best enjoy the Whitsuntidi3 holidays. With the holidays upon us at least a week earlier than last year, and very recent experiences of something nearly akin to arctic weather, there are many who will feel it un- wise to travel far in que§t of change and recreation. In the first half of the present month, the tempera- ture in most parts of the provinces has been low enough to form an appropriate accompaniment to thoughts of turkey, plum puddings, and the other things that tire the youthful imagination at the approach of the festive season in Decemher.The"man in the street"has declared the season to b 3 abnormal while the individual upon whom sits the respon- sibility of saying whether the cold snap was un- precedented, thoughtfully turned to his tomes and his records which, after careful study, only enabled him to say that we were passing through a period of exasperating chilliness by no means unparalleled in proud Albion. But, though the experience has not been devoid of its touch of humour, it has also its serious side. For when the seasons of the year become at variance with the calendar, the eiement of discord is widely ramified. The glorious pageantry of Whitsuntide, as most of us have known it; necessarily suffers from the chilly breath of a winter out of place. Plans Once matured, and afterwards completely upset, mean not only personal discomfort and incon- venience, but more or less of disadvantage to the pockets of the shopkeeper, the agricuiturist,and the vast army of persons who usually thrive at places of public resort under the genial rays of the sun and an alluring canopy of blue. If the north and easterly winds would not cut so keenly, or better still, it the wind would shift a few points, and the sun shine out, our health and pleasure resorts would quickly become very much alive. People need not go abroad to look for amusement at Whitsuntide, or to see thakbeauty dawns bat tardily in England,aud the season " comes but slowly up this way."

It is well that each provincial district, and each Union, should know something of what is being done,in view of the approaching Coronation, for the entertainment of the very poor, and it may be men- tioned here,that;some of the Boards of Guardians are determined that this feature of the general rejoicings shall not only not be neglected, but shall be carried out oq a liberal and even generous scale, and shall apply to both indoor and outdoor poor alike. Such an arrangement is only just and fair. The arrange- ments in some of the unions referred to for men, worn en,and children,have gives considerable satis- faction to the public, but there appears in one or two instances to be the customary "fly in the cream," in the shape of a discrimination in the matter of the outdoor poor. That is to say, the outdoor poor reci- pients of aid under sixty years of age, according to certain local schemes, are to receive no consideration with the exception of the widows and the children. It is, ot course, open to argument whether at a time of what should be an universal rejeicing any exception in regard to age ought to prevail as against any of the outdoor poor. According to these local schemes, imbeciles under the age specified ; men, ordinarily able- bodied,relieved on account of sickness ; the families of men in prison, and the families of soldiers, sailors, and of deserted women should not, in the' opinion of the Guardians, participate in the good things that are to be distributed in honour of the Coronation. Of course, the Guardians in each Union will decide according to their own light, and it would be reasonable to exclude from participation persons known to be of dissolute character, as well as persons certified as belonging to the criminal classes. But the exclusion of individuals coming under the category already alluded to, does not I appear desirable on grounds of public polity, and I possibly steps will yet los taken in these instances to absorb such individuals within the radius of national festivity. Anyhow, there are those of us who hope so.

Lancashire has just efforied one of the mot in- teresting elections to Parliament since the General Election of 1900, and the fact is alluded to in this letter because of the bearing it has upon the dis- cussion of the corn duty proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in which provincial cities and towns especially are so largely interested. The newly elected member has himself assured us that the result turned upon the re-imposed registration duty on corn. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach on Monday evening made the best defence, perhaps, that is possible. But the fact re- mains that someone has to pay, and it makes no difference to the C'aancellor of the Exchequer whether the" someone" is the importer,the trades- man, or the consumer. It is, of course, possibly true that the duty may be paid in part by the foreign producer, who will have to get to the English market. It is useless to dogmatise on a matter of this kind without regard to the position of the market, and the store of the world's wheat supply. But it is perfectly certain that the impost adds a trifle to the price of corn, and other things being equal, the consumer ultimately pays the im- port duty. It has been said, and may be quite true, that the retail price is fixed according to a scale, and that the slight registration duty is not nearly enough to carry the price from the lowest point of what may be described as the fourpenny scale, to the lowest point of the fourpence halfpenny scale; but when the price is near the top of the fourpenny scale,then this impost is enough to turn the balance in favour of the extra halfpenny. So that the tax will in practice be divided between the consumer, who will pay in certain conditions of the market in which there would not formerly have been an ad- vance, and the traders who will have to bear at other times a burden that may be a real hardship, subject always to the possibility that in a season of foreiga abundance and low heights the effect of the duty in England may be minimised. I.;ut the corn duty ought to be resisted, not merely because it is a bad revenue tax, harasses trade and agricul- ture, and draws vastly more money from the people than the treasury will realise, but because it is essentially bad in principle, and injuriously affects the well-being of the very poor by aiding more or less to the price of that which constitutes the principal item of their daily food.

Newspaper readers will remember that several years since a well-known Society lady was severely burned by the ignition of a Celluloid comb, brought about by friction between the comb and the hair Celluloid articles,e FA seen in the shop windows, have continued to be sold just the same,and occasionally other similar accidents have occurred. Celluloid enters into combination with articles of attire.such as collars, as well as combs, and so concerned are certain members of the House of Lords for the safety ot those who wear them, that Lord Saltoun on Tuesday asked the Government to cause such modifications to be made in the manufacture of celluloid articles as would render impossible the serious acidents referred to. Long hours or shop assistants have not half the attraction for lordly sympathisers with the fair sex as the safety of those who affect celluloid combs and collars appears to have. But Lord Belper had a substantial reason for not complying. on behalf of the overnment, with the request that bad been made, since he had been informed that if celluloid was properly manu- factured it would neither explode or take fire except at a very high temperature. So that all the public can do, or that portion thereof who wear celluloid gear, is to see, if they can, that the material put- chased has been properly manufactured.

If heads of families who are just now wondering what the outcome of the Peace Conference at Ver- eeniging will be, had only the" Times "version of the negotiations,they would be disposed to imagine the correspondents of other newspapers had been over-sanguine in stating that there was almost; a certainty of peace being effected and proclaimed in time for the Ring to exercise his clemency in any needful case, on the occasion of his Coro- nation. But the "Times " statement does not I appear to embrace any events beyond the 18th of April, since which date, presumably, many things will have happened ; while, on the other band, authentic advices from Pretoria of later date put a decidedly more hopeful complexion on the situa- tion. For instance, General Wessels, Cthams.ndant Ii Bouwer Jacobs, Louis Botha, Landdrost John Brand, General Wessels, Adjutants John Jacobs, M J Kohler, and John Wessels arrived at Harrismith on Monday, and left by Tuesday morning's train to attend the meeting of delegates at Tereeniging. The names are well worthy of note and being borne carefully in mind. Louis Botha's re-appearance in this connection will be particularly reassuring to most people in this country. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
AN OFFENCE TWELVE MONTHS OLD.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Saturday, before Mr Imison, David Ashley, labourer, of Runcorn, was brought up on a warrant charged with dis- obeying a summons, dated 6tli May, 1901, for using obscene language on the 26th April last year. Ser- geant Gregory proved the case, and prisoner was fined Is and 15s casts. He went to gaol.

div.head: _ FIND OF A DEAD BODY
div.p: _ FIND OF A DEAD BODY

On Sunday evening a fisherman named Bramby found the dead body of a man fhating in the Ship Canal at Inca. The body was in a decomposed con- dition the features being unrecognizable. The de- ceased has every appearance of being a navvy. Two knives and some coppers were in the man's pockets and up to the present the remains have not been identified. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES. . ....

_ At Widnes on Thursday morning, William Con- cannon, Ditton, was charged with deserting his wife a fortnight ago. Mr Peters represented Mrs Concannon. Complainant stated that she had been married seven years, and tilers had been some un- pleasantness. There was one child of the marriage, and two more of a former marriage. A week ago they had words, and defendant left, and had not contributed towards her maintenance. The bench made an order of 103 per week and custody of the child. _ _

div.head: ,-. ALLEGED TFIEFT FROM A WIDNES HOTEL.
div.p: ,-. ALLEGED TFIEFT FROM A WIDNES HOTEL.

Or-i-T-h-u-r-s-d-ay at Widnes before Mr W W Gossage and Mr B Brown, George Will, a stranger, was charged with stealing 20s on Wednesday night from the counter of the Arch Hotel, belonging to Mr Machin. Prisoner entered the bar and asked for drink with a penny. This was refused, and the landlord went to serve some customers in the taproom. Over the counter there were four 20s packets, and upon returning to the bar prisoner ran out. Witness noticed that one had gone and gave chase, securing toe man in Waterloo-road and handing him over to Police Constable Dickson. —Superintendent Keighley asked for .a remand which was granted.

div.head: ANOTHER' DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ANOTHER' DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

On Monday afternoon, at the Runcorn P6lice Court, Mr Robert Dobson. coroner, held an inquest touching the death of William Enapson Williams, steward of the sailing ship Miltiades, who was drowned in the Weston Canal on Friday evening, the 9th inst.—Mr W Shaw was the foreman of the jury.—The evidence showed that the deceased with a man named Thomas Burns, able seaman, went at 8;30 to the Bridgewater Arms and had three glasses of beer each. Taey then parted at 930 deceased going back to his ship. De was then quite sober. In going back to his ship Williams fell into the Weston Canal at 10 p.m. and his cries were heard by two sailors who jumped into the water to rescue the deceased. A. man named Farmer, Rutland-street, also gave assistance but before toey could gat the deceased out of the water he was drowned. There were no marks of violence on the body when it was recovered. A verdict of found drowned was returned the jury complimenting Farmer for his attempt at rescue and regretting that the sailors ware not present that they might be thanked for their ser- vices.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN. Oa Monnay afternoon, at toe Runcorn Police Court, Mr Robert Dobson, coroner, held an inquest touching the death of Annie Barlow, aged 52, wife of Joseph Barlow, Egerton-street, who was found dead at her residence on Sunday morning. Mr W Shaw was foreman of the jury. The evidence showed that the deceased's husband retired to be on Saturday at 11 o'clock, leaving his wife on the sofa, where she usually slept. On Sunday morning when he came downstairs be noticed his wife looked very peculiar, and on a closer examination found her dead and cold.—From the medical evi- dence it was shown that the deceased was in a very emaciated condition, death being really due to a clot of blood on the right side ot the heart.— A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was given.—The husband, relalled, was askei by the Coroner what his wages were ? Witness repiied they did not average 103 a weak, as sometimes he only got 3.3 weekly.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY " Tnisurius."l The spirit of clericalism.is again manifesting itself in Runcorn. This would not be so surpris- ing were Runcorn the only place where the priest demands to exercise his " authority " over civil affairs. It is a remarkable fact that all over the country the spirit of clericalism is slowly but surely permeating the elements of national life. Yet the clog on the wheel of progress that the cleric has been in the past is too well known, even by the superficial reader of history, to need recapitulation. The man in the street knows how the dogmatic parson has done his best to pre- vent freedom of thought and, to strangle Dissent— which really spells liberty—liberty to think, and to act as reason determines. Yet this same spirit that stifled the life of the early church is abroad to-day. The ages have not killed it. Men are still under its spell, and the consequence is that every day the dividing tine is being drawn clearer and sharper marking off two parties which represent clericalism and anti-clericalism. The clericalism of to-day differs but little from the clericalism of the past. The Romish and the Anglican Church have de- veloped the spirit to a nicety. In bath Communions the same inordinate love of power is displayed. The Success of the church does not depend so much on its spiritual life as its power as on organizationt in the numbers it can enroll under its banner; and in its ramifications through society. Every little vantage ground that aids !material power is seized and is immediately turned into a strongeold against its opponents. This plan has been consistently followed out in Runcorn in the case of the Sea- man's Mission, the nurse fund and other organiza- tions which the Anglican party have wrested from the town. Presumably the Cottage Hospital is de- signed to come under the same board of manage- ment and it is not generally known how clericaliz,m tried to sow the seed of discord over the last elec- tion of the chairman of the Council.

--- At the recent School /3oard election the rate- payers became still better acquainted with the tactics of the apostles of clericalism. the Board schools and the work they had performed had to be discredited so that the Voluntary schools might
CRAWFORD7S
RIE AM
CRACKERS
CRISP AND
CREAII'•

rise in public estimation at the expense of their competitors. All the machinery which Jesuitical chicanery could procure was requisitioned. The Boards were denounced as irreligious, and expen- sive; as a needless luxury and not an abiolute necessity. Figured were adduced in support by a clerical of the clericals, Canon Wood, which were proved absolutely incorrect. But the end to be achieved by clericalism was a good (?) one and though the means to accomplish the end might be evil yet the end justified the means ! bus argued the church in an early age; thus has the Jesuit argued at all times; thus has the cleric argued in Runcorn.

Canon Wcod writing in his Church Magazine a week or two ago defended the present education bill very,strongly. It is not, he says, a wanton attack on the Nonconformists at all. " The Bill does not interfere with religious teaching. What the religious teaching is to-day in Voluntary Schools, that it will remain if the Bill becomes law and what in respect of religion the Board Schools are to-day under Boards, that in respect of religion they will remain under the new authorities, sup- posing the new authorities to be called into exist- ence by the passing of the Bill."

Evidently Canon Wood supports the measure and desires all Nonconformists to think that he is a tolerant individual who wishes to respect the religious convictions of all. He holds out, so to speak, the olive branch of peace to Dissenters. And the whole tenour of th 3 paragraph indicates that he desires the people of Runcorn to befieve that, in Church denominational schools he would be the first to allow the child to exercise his conscientious ob- jection to participate in the Church creed Yet is this worthy Canon so tolerant as he professes to bt? Past exp3rience has taught Nonconformists that they can expect little chivalrous treatment at his hands and 'Still less toleration !

I Only a few days after Canon Wool had breathed out to Runcorn Nonconformity peace and good- will, the annual York Convocation was held at 1 which the Canon was present. In discussing the Education Bill the Parliamentary Committee pre- sented a report which contained as its last para- graph the following : "The Committee cannot con- clude this report without stating their opinion that in view of that justice towards others which they demand for themselves, the bill should provide that where there is only one school in a locality, and that in the possession of a particular denomination arrangements shall be secured whereby pupil teachers who may not belong to the denomination may have the benefit of training and experience, and that children not belonging to their denomina- tion may receive alternative instruction in religious knowledge if their parents express a desire for elle) an instruction" Will Nonconformists credit that our broad-minded Vicar, who had recently pro- fessed in his own town love and charity towards Dis4enters, actually seconded an amendment that the clause be deleted ?—an amendment which I if carried into effect, would have the result of making every teacher in such districts either a Churchman or deprive him of technical instruction and a livelihood ; and, further, would force all chil- dren to participate in the church doctrine R at the violation of their principles. The nmen iment was defeated. The Bill itself, in the opinion of the Con- vocation, does not give Diseenters that liberty which Canon Wood asserted it did in his magazine And the Canon, with the majority of the Church- men at the Convocation, must have known it did , not, and evidently intended that it would not be his fault if it did, for he actually seconds an amend- ment to delete a proposed clause that would give the Dissenters that freedom which they desire. If this be not a specious piece of clerical double deal- ing then what, in the ~name of honesty, does straightforwardness mean ?

The latest intelligence shows that the church party are resolved to bin .e the Coronation proceed- ings to a dead lock. Readers will remember that at the town's meetings a general committee repre- senting all the various interests in the town was appointed to organize the proceedings connected with the two days' projected festivities. The com- mittee met in due course and among other things decided, after considerable discussion that the Sunday schools should ballot for the order of procession. Needless to say the proposal to ballot was bitterly opposed by the clerical party. Theirs was the national chutch and in a town's parade it was their " right " to head the processisn. In the ballot, they argue& the Salvation Army might gain the premier position and what a lack of dignity would be there, were they to walk behind the drum and tambourine with their gowned ecclesiastics bringing up the rear. Such a vision was too appalling to contemplate. Their dignity was involved ; their pride was out- raged ; their very existence as a church was threatened by such a procedure. How could they bring up the rear I!! Thus they argued and the reasoning shows stronger than any ilu3tration, thsir arrogance and self assertiveness. Truly in a town's demonstration it seems but just that the oldest school should be given priority over any other and should occupy the premier position as its natural place. Yet " Brunswick," the oldest school, did not ask to lead though it might justly have claimed the honour as is right. If it is a question of the oldest chu-ch leading the van then the Roman Catholic body should be given precedence over all other. Why the National Church, because it is the State church, I should be held to be divinely fitted to take the first place is absurd. So the town's committee thought and as previously stated, it was decided that the ballot should be used as being the fairest method for all the schools concerned. A sub-committee was appdinted of the Sunday School delegates to carry out the ballotting. The delegates met and the first bustness of our worthy Anglican friends, who are generally such sticklers for law and order and the sacredness of the majority, was to pursue obstructionist taetics very similar to those pursued by the irrepressible Irishmen in the House of Com- mons. A couple of hours were wasted in talk and then a resolution was actually made to over-ride the ruling of the General Committee respecting the ballot This was defeated and the committee were on the point of getting to the actual work of balloting for position when a churchman rising in his place gravely informed the committee that on no account could he and his fellow churchmen discuss that business without consulting the clergy The com- mittee broke up in contusion and it is now threatened that unless the Church schools are allowed to head the procession they will have a procession of their own, and, like sulky, spoiled children, bold it all to themselves dissociating themselves altogether from the town's festivities.

--- Such are the tactics of our clerical friends. Use all the legitimate means possible to get your own way but if these fail, still get it no matter how. To carry their point—a point, too, at which nothing is at stake, save their own arrogant intolerance— they would sap the loyalty of every Runcornian ; and would sowdissension between man and man and class ant cla4s. otopus-like this clericalistic spirit embraces everything in its arms. All must be sacri- ficed to satiate its thirst for predominance and power. Reeking with the spirit of intolerance even in civic affairs and drunk with its own self-import- ance the Church body must split Runcorn up into two camps on Coronation day, rather than agree with the ballot method adopted by most of our larger towns Lt the Church have its own belittled parade. Let it hug to itself the thought that it represents the Coronation. To all outsiders such a pitiful action will be the subject for amused contempt end will be a blow at its boasted dignity and prestige from which it will not easily recover.

The town asks all broad tninded Churchmen to put loyalty before sect and if such a course be adopted '.3y Anglicanism, to throw in their lot with the town's procession rather than be controlled by the priest. Obviously the difficulty of Mr Samuel , Taylor's position as chairman of the Council has been vastly increased, ann all true citizens who value the public weal will be only t)o pleased to strengthen his hands at such a critical juncture. Nir Taylor will have the unwavering support of the majority of the ratepayers who place implicit con- fidence in the course he may adopt in dealing with such obstructionists.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DIS- TRICT COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held on Monday even- ing in the Town Hall, Earlestown. Mr T Ormand occupied the chair and there were also present Dr Patterson, Dr Latham, Messrs C B F Boma, C.C., J W Emm-tt, J.P., N Siddeley, W Gilmour, J Simpson, W Thompson,E L Bent.g T Evans, with C Cole (civrk), and R T Surtees (gas and water engineer). ABSENCE OF THE CHAIRMAN. The Chairman announced that he had received a letter from Mr Collingwrol in wnich he desired to ex- press his regret at not beteg able to be present owing to important business engaginents in London.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The letter from Mr E J George (submitted to the last meeting of the Cumcil, and referred to this Committee) with respect to the prevalence and increase of Sunday trading in the district was considered by the committee. ' It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to inform Air George that the police is the prover authority to deal with the matter.—The letters of Police Super- intendent Cocker (which were submitted to the Council at its last meeting) offering to raise donations, 4k.5.. for the provision of a horse ambulance carriage for the district, and t 3 present the same to the Council on certain conditions, were submitted to the Committee. —lt was resolved that the Surveyor be directed to make the necessary arrangements for the houside. of the carriage when presented to the Council.—lt was further resolved that a sum nct exceeding a peony rete be expended by the Coancil on celebrating the Coronation of H.M King Edward VII., and that Councillors W Coiling wood, E V Evans, W Gilmour, Dr Patterson. N Siddeley, and J Simpson. be appointed the sub-committee to carry out the arrange- ments.—The C:erk was instructed to order a new flag for the Town Hall. _

The minutes were approved, on the proposition of the Chairman. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMSIITTEE. ! A letter was road from the director of education for the county, with re4pect to the payment to this Council of a grant, out of the proposed special grant of £2,000, and a ating that to qualify for a share in the special grant, the contributions of the committee for technical instruction purposes must average one halfpenny in the R. The clerk reper:ed that a copy of such letter had been forward° ta the Viaduct Institute Technical In- struction Committee for its observations thereon, and r ad a [-Ver wnicb had beau received from Mr T Ormand, the hon. secretary, stating that the amount contributed oy the committee and by private subscribers amounted to considerable, more than a halfpenny rate. It was resolved that the clerk be instructed to forward such information to the director of education for the co anty, • Dr Patterson moved the confirmation of the minutes and they were unanimmsly agreed to.

GAS COMMITTEE. INCREASE IN TFIE PRICE OF GAS. The monthly report of the gas engineer was read,from which it appeared that of the ordinary meters in use 1,060 were dry aad 260 wet, and of the automatic ro-t-rs 1,476 were dry and 12 wet, or out of a total of 2,798 meters 9.75 per cent wire wet. At a special m•eting of the Gas Committee held on Monday afternoon, it was rosolved that from and atter the Ist July next ail charges for gas los increased by twopence per thousand cubic feet.—The Clerk presented a report to the committee relating to the practice in other towns with reference to the hlrln2 of gas ,toves. It was res iived that there ha an exhibition of cookie,' stoves at the Town flail ho that t following firms be invited to exnibit sce;irnens of their work: Messrs F.etcaer, Ru4sell, and Company (Warrington). Messrs li,chmond and Company, Limited (Warrington), and Messrs Wright. and Company (Rirminghim).

It was also decided that the stoves be let out on the five years' hiring system and that the stoves be fixed and maintained free of charge.-4113 Clerk also presented his report upon the accouute of the gas department for the year ended 31st filarch, 1902. It was resolved that it be a suggestion to the Finance Com- mittee to transfer £5OO trona the district funds account ot the general department to the gas department on ! acceunt of the cost of lighting the streets in the district. ' —A letter was read from the Vulcan Foundry Com- pany stating that as the bulk of the gas to be supplied Ito them would be required for heating purposes and for ' gas engine toey inquired whether it coal I not be sup- plied at a special rata.—lt was resolved that the Clerk inform the Company that the matter will be considered as soon SI Mr Thompson is lved the confirmation ef the minutes. ' Mr Edimett thought the resolution rospeetiog the hire of gas stoves would lead the public astray. Toe stoves i would n it be pr )vided and fixed free unless the amount of piping required was lee than 30 feet. If more 1 pipleg than that was required it would have to be paid for by the hirer of the stove. Toe Chairman said he was glad Mr Emmett had raised the point. It was only intended to allow 30 feet of pip- ing free of charge. Dr Latham called attention to the fact that only a portion of the engineer's report appeared on the agenda. 113 criticised the attitude of the committee in keeping the public in the dark respecting what was bsine done a^ the gas works It was contrary he said,to the wishes of the gas committee that the public who would be called upon to pay the increased price of gas, should know the workings of the gas workl, it was °batters. to the com- mittee's wishes that the public should facilitate cho work of the committee, and it was also contrary to the wishes of the committee that the public outside snould know anything whatever ot the engineer. The minures were then passed, WATER EXTENSIONS.—A WATER TOWER TO BE PROVIDED.

At a meeting of the Water Committee, the Clerk reported that be had prepared moo,randum of agree- ment with the Elaydock Urban District Council by which doh Council granted permisqien fo: that C)uncil to surinly water to the premises known as the " Wood- land,,," Ashton-road, on certain cmditions, which mensorand ,m had been forwarded to the hlaydock Council for it approval, before construction of the works At a meeting of the water special sub-committee On Monday af cerneon, the reports of Allows Read and Waring and of tire. Clerk and engineer with respect to their inspection of the ferro coacrate water tower at Bournemouth were read, from which it appeared that ferr concr,te was a euitable material with which to construct the water tower at the pumping station. It was resolved that the reports be approved and that the Water Committee be recommended to erect a tower of ferro concrete. At a meeting of the Wet q. Committee, the same after- noon, Mesirs Read and Waring ware instructed to com- plete the water scheme by the preparation of plans and estimates for a water tower to be constructed of ferro concrete at the pumping station with a capacity of 300,000 gallons and for the materials required in connection therewith. Dr Latham. in answer to a question, was informed that the agreement with the flay dock Counail had not been completed. The Mihail-CPS were confirmed. HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr Watkins in his report to the abtve mentioned committee stated that the birth rate was 30'3 and the death rate 11.3 per 1,000 of the e•timated population. Eighteen cases of infectious sickness were notified to him and five of these Cases were sent to the isolation hospital. Alet ir was read frim Ai -sirs .1 Mainwaring and Co., o Warrington, enclosing a claim of Mr C H Marsh against the Council, amounting to £lO2 1O 103, for damage to Lois crops and land, caused by the taking of the sewer pipe from Mill-lane to the outfall works. It was resolved that the Surveyor be instructed to see the valuers with respect to their 'claim, and to report to this committee thereon. These minutes were confirmrd. THE CORONATION.—THE MARKETS. The Clerk read an order issued by Vie L scat Govern meet Board relating to the payment out of the rates of expenses in connection with the Goronation. The order, he said, did not legalise any expenditure, but preven- ted any disallowance by the diqrict auditor. The Click also reported that it was toe opinion of the Coronation sub-committee that the Market should be held on the Wednesday preceding the day of the Corona- tion and closed on the Thursday and Ftiday in Corona- tion week. It would be necessary for the Council to sancion the alteration. Mr Gilmour spoke in support of the alteration, which was approved of. DR. PATTERSON CONGRATULATED.

- - The Chairman thought the Coupcil ought not to separate before offering a word of congratulation to Dr Patterson, who had been paid the compliment of being asked to preside over the Board of Guardians for the Warrington Union. Dr Patterson was not a man of many words, but he attended to his duties, and they were glad to know that the services he had rendered the Union in general and Warrington in particular. had at last been recognised by his appointment as Chairman of the Hoard of Guardians. lie (Mr Ormand) begged to offr the Council's hearty and sincere congratulations on the honour conferred upon him. Mr Gilmour added his c mgratulations. Dr Patterson, in responding, thanked the Council for their kind expressions and expressed the hope that he would be able to do his duty in his new office.

Prescot Agricultural Show. The annual snow of the Prescot Agricultural Society was held in Knowsley Park on Thursday. Unfortunately the weather proved most unfavour- able. The entries for horses exceeded last year by fifty-one, and included the principal prize-winners of the North of England. The total number of entries was 1,116, against 1,174 in the previous year. The decrease of fit tv-eight occurred chiefly in the small- stock class. Mr H R d'A Willis presided at the unch held in the show grounds.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOwN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOwN.

If the public will generously assist the movement the provision of a Cottage Hospital for the districts of Earlestown and Newton is likely to become an accomplished fact. For some time past the idea of holding a three days' bazaar has possessed the minds of many ladies, and of several members of the Committee, and with this object in view many hours of untiring labour have been spent. The Committee appointed to co operate with the ladies is taking the matter in hand with energy and zeal, and is determined no efforts shall be spared to make the affair a real success. An open air bazaar will be somewhat of a novelty in the neighbour- hood, and because of this the Committee anticipate an unqaalified success. There will be plenty of amusement for the public and if the weather be fine, people will have an opportunity not only of spending plenty of money but an enjoyable time.

I am afraid the need for a ratepayers' association in Earlestown will be very much felt in the near future,if the actions of the District Council are not criticised. The price of gas is going up,the Council having decided to raise it by two pence per 1000 feet, which will make the charge to consumers 3s 21 per 1000. One would not grumble muck if the quality was commensurate with the price, but it is not, and hers is the rub. They ~ay the gas works are being worked at a loss, and I suppose the Council are determined to get something more out of the consumer.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

The second team received a visit fro— the Aig- burth second string, at Newtm, and al ”nough the issue was much narrower than that between the first teams, still they managed to obtain the victory by 78 runs to 72. S Barr, a pramising young player, totalled 28.

EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The 16611 quarterly meeting of the members of this Society was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. Mr D Forrester presided, but there was not a large attendance. The repors and statement of accounts showed that the receipts for the quarterlamounted to £13.339 153 7d, being an increase over last quarter of £1,238 Is 7d. The net profits realised were .£2,088 17s Hid, which it was proposed to dispose of by paying a dividend of 3s in the £, absorbing £2,033 17s. The balance of £35 IN nil, woll/d be divided as follows :—£2o to Workmen's Compensation fund, £lO to Dividend Reserve fund and the balance £25 Os Hid, to Continwnt fund. Durinz the quarter 74 new members had been admitted, and 26 had withdrawn leaving 1809 on the register, 1404 of whom hat brought in checks. The balance sheet was con sidered very satisfactory and was foram:oly adopted. Messrs Cave and J013.0A were re-elected to the Com- mittee of Managemeni, Mr C Conway was appointed members delegate to the C. W.S. quarterly meeting. The usual grant of 7s 6d per head was made in connection with tha employs annual trip. Mr J El Mullins was aopointi.d to attend the Inter- nation Co-operative Congress to be held at Exeter. It was stated that the proposed treat to the chil- dren of members, wonld take place on July 12th in the Society's own field, and that a charge of a penny would be made for each ticket issued.
!working Men's Mission, Bank_ Quay.

The Bank Quay Working Men' Mission Sunday school held its school anniversary, on Sunday. The preacher in the morning was Mr C C Hulbert, of Didsbury Col- lege, who gave a very prae'icable discourse on " Is the young man Absalom safe." In the afternoon, a service of song was rendered by the children, and choir, entitled " Michael's Motto,' and the con- nective reading was given by Miss E The production was really splendid, and was listened to earnestly, by a large congregation In:the evening, the chapel was cTowlod, many having, to go back. Toe preacher, was the Rev C H Hocken, who cielived a very profitable sermon, on " Train up a child, in the way it should go, and when it is old, it will not &put from it." The singing was excellent and plainly showed that toe choirma,t =r, must have gone to some trouble. to obtain such nerf'ctiorr. The soloists, Miss Lucy Davies (soprano', of Hollinfare. and Miss lily Foden (contralto), of Warrington, ren- dered beautifully the solo parts of tho anthem " Hark, hark my soul." Throughout the day the whole of the services were greatly enjoyed. The collections for the day realised £l2 51, and the Committee thank all those who have Coma forward to mike the anniversary a SUCCESS.

KEEPING UP APPEARANCES —ASYLUM ATTENDANT STE/LS A PICYCLE. At the Warrington Occesioaal Court on Monday, before Hr A Frost, William Peat. au attendant at Winwick Asylum, was charged with stealing a bicyle, of the vsslna of £7, the property of Thomas Hazeldine, from outside the , Longford Hotel on the 8/h May.- He p'eaded guilty.— Thomas Hazeldine. a ston.m tson, 'Rinsvick Quay, Winwiek. stated that he left the bicycle outside the Longford Hotel at about 9 20 and when he came out e the building at eleven o'clock the bicycle was missing. Witness was in Collins-lane on Sunday and saw the prisoner riding the bicycle, tie ran &Car him and told him it was his machine. Prisoner said he had had it, for a long while Witness then cal'ed P.C. Sharp and Peat was taken into crt,tody.—P.C. aloarp sat' be was in Collins-lane at aboat 8.30 an Sunday evening and saw prisoner riding a bicycle in company with a young lady. Hezeldine came to him and said the Prisoner was en his bieye• Witness and Haz4dine gave chase and everaook the prisoner who was going in the 'Urea-ion of BariestOwn. The prisoner said he bad had the bicynle a long time,and bad get it ; frcm a man Liside the Asylum. He refused to give his name. risoner afterwards laid he had stolen the bicycle to" keep Hp appearaeces."—He was remanded to the War- rington County Petty Sessions to be held next Wednesday. SeLDIPRS' DIsGEACEPEL CoNDUCP,-OBiTIVICTION AND ASSAULT. At the Warrington Police Court on Monday ,before Mr If Monks and other magistrates, Thomas Nugent and John Cnnlan, private soldiers, from Nrford Barracks, were charged w'th having been drunk and disor ierly in Winwick-s reet at 25 minutes pat ten oa Sunday night. They pleaded go lty. Coalan, who appeared in the dock in khaki, was also charged with having oastructed P.C. Metcalf whilst in the execution or his duty, and Nugent was also with having assaul- ted Henry Cheeney in 9cotland-road.—P C. Metcalf said he was on iluty In Horsemer cet-street at the time stated and saw a crowd of po pie et the end of Bewsey-street. He went there and found he prisoners and another soldier qn srrsll- lug. He asked them to go away and the third man Bug- gestei to the prisoners that they should do so. Nugent swore arid said "No fear." He added that if they could not stand together in the street Without witnees coming and interfering, he wonld upset him. The others took him along the street but he tore himse'f away and came back to withess. Witness took him into custolv, whereapon he threw himself down and b•carne very violent Conlan repeatedly tried to release Nugent. Witness struggled with them some con- siderable time, an 4 P C Gilchrist then came up. Conlan made off, but was even`Loally caught by Constables Whitby fond Turner. He rslnsed to give any account of C Whitby said he saw the lest witaess with Nugent in custody. He arrested Conlan, who welt quietly until they got Into Ssotland-road. He there threw tarn 'elf -town and became very violent. P 0 Turner and Henry Chesney came to the assietaace of witness They had to carry the prisoner the greater part co, the w yto the Police station. At one time helgot his leg loose and kicked Cheeney violently on the side of the face 13 ith prisoners were very drunk—k' C Turner gave corroborative evidence.--Etenry Cheeney,engine driver 133. Londord-stre-t, said he saw tVhitby struggling with Conlan ins Scotland-road and wont to his assistance. Prisoner was very violent and kicked witness on the side of the face, marking him It was with great difficuby that they got him to the police station.—Nugent said he met a few friends and got a" sup "too much.—Conlan sai he had a few pints too ranch He was very sorry for what had onourred.—TheChiet Constable stated that he had the men's army character sheets. Conlan joined the depot on March 29th of this rat.. He had been once absent from duty and bad broken out of the barracks when a prisoner. Nugent had on one occasion been found in possession of intoxicating drink in the barrack room.—Nugent was fined Is and costs, and Coultas 10a awl costs. The Chairman said the Bench were very much obliged to Cheeney for the assistance he had given to the poace. and they were very sorry that he had been mauled In consequence of it.

Senor Severo, tLa nvent-ir of a flying machine, and his engineer, met terrible deaths in Paris on Monday, the airabip being wteck^d by an explosion. while 1,500 feet from the ground. The inventor and Li companion were dashed to the ground, beta their bodies being picked up shockingly cautils,ted. The accident was witnessed by the aeronaut's wife, family, and friends. At St. Helens Police Court on Monday, William Huy- ton was fined £25 and costs for acting as a broker without a licence. Evidence was given that the defend- ant purchased lead from boys, who bad stolen .it from braises in course of erection.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
THE trouble with some folks is that they believe so much more than they hear. "'Ls not in mortals to command success," but any man with a little nerve can predict it.

SOME of the folks who complain of being mis• understood are simply unintelligible. HIS TROUBLE.—" Can't he support his wife?" "Oh, he can support her all right, but he corn. plains that she is insupportable !" BENNY DICTIIS : "What do you do when your wife cries for money?" Wellwed : "Oh I I have a way of applying a cheque to her tears." THE PHILISTINE: "Is it true that genius is only a capacity for taking pains?" The Poet: "No. True genius is the ability to write fly-time poetry in the middle of winter."

THE DIFFERENCE. —"I have learned a new dis- tinction between pessimist and optimist." "What is it?" "A pessimist always calls cream milk,' and an optimist always calls milk ' cream.' " ETHEL : "Are you sure that all his thoughts are of you?" Edith: "Oh, yes I Why, he has just lost his position on account of inattention to busi- ness !"

"JERKIN'S wife is very strict with him." "in what way?" "She charges him a penny every time he says a bad word, and she won't let him have seven for sixpence." "OH, I don't know about Kipling I He's not 90 extremely successful. A single line brought me in a couple of thousand not long ago." "A single line?' " Yes ; a railway line that I had sued for compensatory damages. A PROFESSIONAL VIEW.—It is the profound conviction of the average shoemaker that the ii)icy- cle is a very dangerous machine, and that riding is not nearly so healthful an exercise as pedes- trianism. A FAVOURITE.—Mrs. Smallcannon : "I see you are as much of a gallant with the ladies Eta ever —Major Slamjammah : " Indade, that was always a strong wakeness with me." HER BAROMETER SPOILED.—MTS. 110ggS : " Why do you dislike Dr. Curem ? " Mrs. Muggs : " He cured my husband's rheumatism, so he can never tell when it is going to rain, and last week I spoiled a brand new hat." A LumNous VERDICT. —A coroner's jury in a rural distriet returned the following verdict : "That the deceased came to his death by trying to light his pipe with an electric light, which can't be done successful." HER FATE--Mrs. De Work: "I have trained my eldest daughter into a thorough housekeeper. There is nothing she does not know." Miss Da Flight : "What a nice, handy maiden aunt she will make for your other daughters' children !" WARNING TO OTHER LITTLE BIRDS. —" Oh, Georgie I Who opened the canary's cage ?" "I did. You told me a little bird was a-whispering to you when I was naughty, so I knew it inu:it be him, as there was no other little bird about. So 1 opened the cage, and the cat's eaten him. That's what he's got for splitting on me." INFECTION.—Irishman : "Oi feel very quare, docthor. Oi belave oi'm pain' to have hydrophoby." Doctor: "Have you been bitten by a mad dog, then ? " Irishman: "Not exactly ; but about foive years ago oi' was bit by a flea that oi belays had been bitin' a dog that afterwards went mad." A SCOTSMAN, living in the West Indies, was much distressed by Sabbath-breaking. One Sun- day, going home from meeting, he saw a small negro fishing, and began to lecture him, winding up with "No good boy goes fishing on the Sab- bath, and "—warming up—" no good fish will bite on the Sabbath." "No, massa, no," replied the boy, "but dis chile fishin' for debbil fish, ear." "WHAT do you mean," said the father, "by keeping lae hours in this way 1" "I'm sowing my wild oats," replied the young man. " that's it, eh I" continued the parent, disclosing a whip. "Well, here's where we do some thrashing." AUTHOR: "What do you think of my new book ? " Friend: "It certainly contains much food for thought." Author: "Do you really think so?" Friend: "Yes, but it seems to have . _

been wretchedly cooked." "DAN," said a four-year-old to his brother, "give me a penny to buy a monkey." "We have one monkey in the house already," said his brother. "Who is it, Dan?" "It's you," was the reply. "Then, Dan, give me a penny to buy nuts for the monkey." The brother could not resist this appeal. Miss Jriaws was out walking with an admirer on each side. A storm came on, accompanied by lightning. Jones said he was frightened. Brown thought it a capital opportunity to show off his superior courage before the adored one. "What are you frightened at? Jam as cool as a cucumber." "Yes, I should not fear," replied Jones, "if. you and I were alone, but I am afraid of Miss Jinks in this lightning;_ she is so attractive." Brown is still a bachelor, but Jones is not. MR. RENNEY SANCE : "Now, where would you prefer the drawing-room ? " Mr. Strukile : "Look here, young man, I've let you put up a smokin'• room, when I don't smoke; a music-room, when I couldn't play a mouth-organ; a nursery, when I ain't got no nurse; and a pantry, when I don't pant; but I'm goin' to draw the line at a draw- ing-room, when I couldn't even draw a straight SHOPMAN (after very considerable trouble in dis- arranging his window): "That's the necktie you mean, I think, sir—the bright green and scarlet. Anything else to-day, sir?" isEithetic Person : "Oh, I wouldn't touch the horrible thing. Only you say, 'Any article willingly taken from the window,' and that awful necktie offends my artistic tastes. Good-day.' TAKING HIS PlCK.—Eager Inquirer: "Are there any good mining locations still open up there?" Returned Klondiker : "I should say so. You dan go there and take your pick." Eager Inquirer : "Great Scott ! If I can go and take my choice" --Returned Klondiker : "I didn't eav that. I said you could take your pick; but you'll have to use it in somebody's else's diggings." Eager In- quirer "Oh !" THE Grand Vizier was sceptical. "The Chris- tian powers," hu argued, "still show their teeth upon occasion." "Oh, they're probably adver- • tising somebody's dentifrice 1' replied the Sultan, who had a few more subjects he desired much to massacre, and who, accordingly, was extremely loth to admit that European disarmament and universal peace were only chimerical dreams. WHAT HE Mmonv EAT.—Abernothy, being called to a patient who fancied himself ill, told him what he thought, but would not prescribe. "Now you are here," said the patient, " I shall be obliged if you would tell me how I must live—what I may eat and what I may not." My directions as to , that point," said the doctor, "will be few and simple. You must not eat the poker, or the tongs, for they are hard for digestion; nor the bellows, because they give you the wind; but anything else you please." 808 burst into the house in a state of high ex- citement. His hands and clothing were smeared with a liberal amount of sticky substance, and his face wore a glow of triumphant satisfaction. "I ' say, mother; those new people across the road don't know much I" he exclaimed. " They've got a notice on their front door that says 'Wet , Paint.'" "And you've been getting into it ! You ought to be ashamed of yourself 1" said his mother, severely. "That notice was put up to warn people to keep away from it." "Yes, I know, persisted Bob, with the enthusiasm of a ' rightly rewarded investigator. "But it wasn't paint, and I proved it. It's only varnish !" WORKS BOTH WAYS.—" You're nervous," saip the doctor. "Quite right," admitted the patient. " That's why I sent for you." "The only thing for you to do," explained the doctor, " is to give up smoking entirely." "I don't smoke at all," answered the patient. "Ah !" said the doctor; "then the thing for you to do is to smoke a good cigar or a pipe occasionally. It has a very soothing effect." It's so easy to prescribe when you know how.

THE late Prince Bismarck is credited with a splendid mot. Owing to the state of his nerves, km had for some weeks given up his cigar and his glase of wine. He mentioned the circumstance to the Emperor William 1., who pooh-poohed the idea of its necessity. "Why, look you," said his Majesty, "I am ever so much older than you, yet smoke my cigar, and drink my glass of wine, and find myself not a jot the worse for it." "Cer- tainly," replied the Chancellor, "but it is ti,n old story—the rider can always take things easier than the horse." THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.head: NEW NOVELS,
div.p: NEW NOVELS,

MACMILLAN AND CO.—There is a fascinating frestinees in Miss Una L Silberrads new novel, "Princess Puck," (pp 410 60.) which the reader can hardly resist. It holds him to the story in pleasant bonds, the which he would not voluntarily break. " Princess Puck "is essentially a study of one per- son. Her three euitorcone of whom alone is really and truly her lover, though each of the three is temporarily fascinated, her aunt and cousins, and her vicar, though depicted firmly.are all subsidiary in interest to herself. The same remark applies to the local setting. We are told thet this represents East Angiii, but it might almost as well be written of any part of the English coast within a short railway journey of London, Wilholmina Alardy, familiarly know as " Bill " is Princess Puck indeed, active, efficient, and comprehending. She is a creature of infinite charm, but her passion for plain and grubby hard work, her alluring geniality and beautiful voice, are combined with such dar- ing wit and unconventionality tbat it is easier to feel her fascination than to believe in her ultimate happiness even with Kit Harborough. Miss Si:- berrad's feeling for the eternal youth of the world :is keen, and her power to express it unusual. At times thiKi expression is even intense, as when Wilhelmina electrifies (in very different degree and kind) all the guests.at a stiff tea-party by her ring- ing of a rare old love ditty, and in the description of the first meeting of Princess Puck and Kit. Humorous passages abound, and situations are never over-explained, and the English throughout is of excellent quality. Those people who have a liking for Crockett and who admired "The Raiders," will probably enjoy " The Dark o' the Moon," being certain further his- tories of the name folk. Like its predecessor it is full of incident, which is woven round the fortunes of the Faa's Hector, John and Joyce, while the hero, who tells the story, is of rather a wishy-washy type. Modestly enough he disclaims all preten,ion to heroism, but the reader cannot help wishing he would occasionally do something sufficiently gallant and daring as to justify his position in the story end to deserve the love which the charming Joyner bears for him. Th«ro are a large number of other characters playing subsidiary parts fairly well, but, if anything the book errs on the side of verbosity. The deeds of the Amazonian maid Marion could just as well be omitted, though the reader regrets to part with Eppie,her entertaining parent with a tongue as keen as her heart is tender, The Faa's themselves supply a current of keen interest, just as in the " Raiders " Presumably, we have now finished with them, for John, the Ring of Little Egypt, and Hector the outlaw both die fight- ing shoulder to shoulder in" The Dark o' the Moon" (pp .511,. 691.

—he incidents of Michael Ferrier, by E Frances Poynter (pp 307, 68), could easily be compressed hit° the ten or a dozen pages of an ordinary maga- zine story. There are only seven cberaaters of tbe slightest importance, and their individualities, though strongly marked, are not patticalarly original- The story has no moral, and no epigram- matic sayings or brilliant conversations, but the book is by no means a bad one. A poet, who is a genius. and a member of Parliament, who is commonplace, ." are rivals for the hand of a young girl -whose sole 'guardians are an elderly maiden lady and an absentee rake of a father. Des- pite the schemes of tne commonplace suitor's mother the girl accepts the genius In a quarrel, which takes place without the knowledge of any third person, the accepted lover more or less acci- dentally shoots his rival. The heroine hears the r truth from him, but marries him in spite of it. Remorse for the murder so works upon a contunip- Live constitution that he dies soon after the marriage and just before the inquiries set on foot by the mother of tbe dead man have succeeded in bringing the crime home to him. By far the best- drawn characters in the book are the consmonplace member of Parliament, a young man who has given up his life to the study of goad manners and the formation of correct tastes, and his clecer and superficial mother, who has devoted herself to the attainment of comfort and amusement for ber son and herself. A well-developed story, truthfully de- lineated characters, and correct English are things which should go far to make the book successful even it it does not show _signs of any great origin- ality in conception or plot.

div.head: NOTES ON CIAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON CIAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Cricket. Local cricket enthusiasts who witnessed Saturday' match at the Arpley enclosure had no cause to be d. appointed with the display of the Warringtonia Bootle were the visiting eleven, and after a highly i teresting contest, retired defeated to the tune of 5 runs. The home team are entitled to hearty congra lations on their achievement, for Bootle had unusually strong contingent doing duty, and came Warrington with a good record.

Batting first, the visitors were all dismissed for ti... small total of 39. The Warrington bowlers - Lynes a Bibby were in capital form and their efforts were su pj ported by remarkably smart fielding. Mason, t Bootle professional, and T W Crouch, were the oak batsmen who gave much trouble. Mason's innings ha 4 realised 14 when he was caught by Bibby, and erou was responsible for 9 not out. Lynes and Bib wrought much havoc with the ball, the profession accounting for 5 wickets at a cost of 22 runs whi the local captain's average was even more creditable, being 5 wickets for 16 runs.

Mention should be made of the fine catches amou' Oohed by several of the Warrington men, Briggs is performing a surprising feat in taking the ball high up with oae hand after having apparently misjudge its flight.

The Warrington innings was productive of 96 runs, most of the batsmen acquitting themselves well. Callon and P B Hawtin commenced, the bowling being shared by Mason and J W Smith. With seven runs on their score sheet Callon was taken at point and Lynes fillet! the vacancy.. Both batsmen were in a merry mood anal runs came very freely, the professional earning a ring.' ing cheer when he lifted a ball from Smith clean over the old pavilion. Thirty was sent up as a result of twenty minutes play, but four runs later Lynes, in jumping out to Mason, missed, and was smartly stumped.

Hawtin was now joined by B Silcock, and the Bootle aggregate was passed without further loss. Smith was relieved by Crouch, but runs continued t coins steadily and the total was taken to 53 before Hawtin was caught at third man. •The retiring batsman had made 19 by stylish cricket.

Disasters now befel the locals, for in quick succession J Thompson, J Briggs, C Goodall and G Hampson wern dismissed, whilst at 68 Silcock failed in a short run and retired for a patiently played 16. Some vigorous hitting by J Gibbon caused Bootle further trouble and he was eventually caught on the boundary for a speedily coin' piled sixteen. J W Bibby brought up the rear, but sal( W Podmore caught at cover, the innings realizing 96.

By the narrow margin of eight runs, Sankey Wire Mills accounted for Cheshire Lines Engineers. Wood- cock headed the score sheet for the visitors, his inningg realizing 29 and Burton also did k ood service, knocking up 20. Howard and P R Lawless and Duckworth were to the fore on the Engineers' side scoring 18, 16 and 11 respectively. P R Lawless bowled with the most effect, his average being five wickets at a cost of three runs. -- Latchford Baptists scored a signal success at Lowton- The villagers were all dismissed for 33 and to this Or visitors had responded with 117 for the loss of eigli wickets when stumps were drawn. J Hallam did re° markably good work with both the bat and the ball. compiling 55 not out, and taking 7 wickets for 13 runs - J. Lester also batted well, rattling up 25.

Peter Walker and Son's Eleven encountered Strettoll and Appleton, C.C., and defeated them by the majority of 32. C Hallows who scored 11 fer the losers was the only batsman to attain double figures. W. Ashtoll bowled remarkably well, capturing 7 wickets for 10 runs.

Cycling. To the joy of cyclists, the weather on Saturday took a complete change for the better, and during the after- noon and evening wheeling was exceedingly pleasant. The members of the Warrington club went to Davenham• Sixteen turned out, and greatly enjoyed the ride, which was made via Weaverham and Vale Royal, the countrY in that part of Cheshire looking at its very best at pre- sent. Arrived at the Bull's Head, the party adjourned to the Bowling Green, where the second of a series of bowling handicaps for this season was played off. Some exciting -encounters were witnessed, and at the finish the result was found to be :-1, W Taylor ; 2, G White- house ; 3, Pickavance, jun ; and 4, W Brown. Art excellent tea was provided by Host Latimer, and after- wards the party commenced the return journey, and arrived in Warrington about 10 p.m.

An international contest took place at Paris ou Saturday for the much-coveted record of one hour Representatives of five nations competed as follows Torn Linton (England), Elkes (America), Robl (Ger- many), Dickentmann (Rolland), and Taylor (France). Elkes got the lead, but was almost immediatelY challenged by Linton, who raced him, amid great ex- citement, to a standstill. Linton was then challenged by the German, and for a matter of ten kilometre neither could gain any visible advantage. Dicken.t- mann fell, and was rather badly bruised, and big machine was smashed. The unfortunate rider wag helped off the course by police agents. At 50 kilometrFs Linton, who had remained uripassed,spurted forward 10 resolute style and beat off one by one all his opponents- He covered 71 kilometres,99s metres in one hour, there- by exceeding his previouslrecord by 4 kilometrea The victor,in capital condition, carried in his own machine, and told a press correspondent that on a future may sion he would get up to a record of 80 kilometres.

A terrible accident occurred on Tuesday, on the cycln track at Atlantic City. A well-known cyclist named Archie M'Facheria was being paced by a motor, when the machinery went wrong and the car stopped- ArFachern, who was going immediately behind it, dashed into the car. Be was terribly injured about the chest, and died shortly afterwards.

Sir,—l am pleased to see that the letter of your correspondent, Andrew Striven, has produced some fruit ki the communications from Henry Gandy and Ed ard T Reed which you printed last Saturday. The matter to which the writers draw 3ttention is of the gravest importance as affecting the honour of God and the welfare of the town. If the Churches and Chapels are of any use at all there must be, as Mr Reed says, "A number of people who hold with intense Conviction the belief that the weekly day of rest—is fraught with great blessings to the physical and mental nature of man." This is as it should be, for the Sabbath was designed to convey such blessings. Through disobeying a Divine command the father of our race and all his posterity were doomed ton life of toil which should only terminate in the grave. But the merciful Being who imposed the penalty accompanied it with the priceless boon of one entire day's rest in every seven. And the , weary, heavy-laden and poorly rewarded workers in our fields, mines and manufactories alone can realise the true value of that boon. How lamentable it is then to find a growing tendency on all hands to minimise, If not altogether abolish, the appointed time for rest. Thousands of men on the railways, thousands in the public houses, and thougands of men and hokum in our street carriages are compelled to labour on the Sundays as if the Fourth Commandment bad never been written. Even in War- rington, where religious appliances are so numerous.the Town Council, not content with open drink shops and omnibus traffic have now given a new and attractive impetus to Sunday profanation by the running of electric cars during the whole of that day. As these oars are run for money one is tempted to suspect that the new venture is intended to help the Corporation which, like the Tory Government, seems to thrive most in a state of debt. But suppose this is denied and we are told that the Sunday. cars ply for the benefit of the public what then ? Is it not a matter of history that a loyal observance of .the day of rest brings peace and prosperity to a nation, and that its profanation is accrompaniediby demoralization and disaster. The Jews, scattered as they .are all over the world, continue to observe the Sabbath as a day of rest and worship. And Christians of all denominations profess to do so too, although they have changed the day for keeping it. But when one looks at the law itself one is struck be the peculiar methods of the Christians in dealing with it. It is recorded on Divine authority that we cannot serve God and Mammon at the same time. But a great number of modern Christians appear to believe that they can do both on Sundays. They find it very agreeable to rest froth their work and enjoy the discourses called sermons on those days, while their beware of wood and drawers of water are debarred altogether from rest and worship. This way of keeping holy the Sabbath day is very popu- lar; but What is highly o-teemed among men is abomina- tion with God. That gracious Being is no respeotor of persons, and the requirements of His Sabbath Law are dishonoured and not obeyed by the simultaneous sounds of labour and 'psalm-singing on the day appointed for rest. And moreover, if it is permissible for Town Coun- cillors or any other men to secularise the Christian Sabbath one would suppose that they might secularise the Churches and Chapels too. For the law which enjoins worehip is the same law which forbids all manner of wcrk on the Sabbath day.—Yours truly. I ONA.

div.head: Return of Sergeant Price, of Warrington. Enthusiastic Scenes.
div.p: Return of Sergeant Price, of Warrington. Enthusiastic Scenes.

There were scenes of great rejoicing at Warring- ton on Monday night,when Sergeant William Price, who has served at the front for over two years returned home. Sergeant Price who, prior to his departure for the Cape, was employed at the works of Messrs Pearson aad Knowles, left Warrington in November 1899 with the let South Lancashire reservists, and has been through many im- portant engagements including Spion Kop. For his conduct in the latter action he was mentioned by General Buller in his despatches to the Secretary of State for War as follows :- 4, Ist Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, 2,573. Sergeant Price, 24th January. Spion Kop. Con- spicuous bravery in centrolling his section under very heavy fire, and as a Volunteer, traversed 200 yards under a very heavy fire to assist a signaller." He also volunteered to assist Col Thorneycroft to search the trenches, where they found the position to be an untenable one. His gallant conduct earned for him the Distinguished Conduct Medal. Sergeant Price's time as a reservist has now expired and his , relatives and numerous friends have been rejoiced by his return borne safe and sound. Telegrams received on Sunday and Monday by Sergeant Price's parents, who reside at 34, Walker- street, contained the welcome information that he would arrive at the Central Station on Monday night. Half-past nine was the time mentioned in the telegram received on Monday afternoon,and the news of the approaching return of Sergeant Price having become known to many of his friends pre- parations were quickly in progress for the purpose of giving him a nandsome reeeption.Walker-sr. was soun gaily decorated with flags,and long before 9 30 hundreds of people had assembled on the platform of the Central station and in the street below. The members of the Borough Band were also in attend- ance and played one or two pieces pending the arrival of the train, which at length steamed into the station-But a disappointment awaited the crowd as the sergeant did not make his appearance. Elopes , were entertained that he would arrive by another train which was expected in a few minutes, but when the train arrived it was found that the ser- geant was not included among the passengers. The company's time table was consulted,and it was soon made evident that he would arrive by the train due at 10 30, and when it steamed into the station cheers from those at the further end of the platform proclaimed the fact that Sergeant Price had at last arrived. Scenes both affecting and enthusiastic were wit- nessed,and the fervent greetings over, the hero of the hour was raised to the shoulders of a couple of stalwart friends and carried down the platforml steps into the street below. To the strains of "Seel the Conquering Hero Comes," and the shouts of the crowd, the sergeant was carried shoulder high along Winwick-street, Orford-lane, Silver-street,into Win • wick-road, thence up Tanners-lane, and Bewsey- street to Walker-street. Here a large crowd had assembled, and when the sergeant arrived deafening cheers were raised. At the call of his' friends Sergeant Price made a short speech, in which he expressed the pleasure it afforded him to have been so cordially received on his return home after such a long absence. He added that this was his second attempt at speech-making, the first one being when he left the works at Defiant. Going outside to say "Good- night "to the crowd Sergeant Price said : " Again I thank you for your kindness. I am glad to get back to Warrington. There is no country like Eng- land, and no town like Warrington. Ido not wish to leave it again. Good-night to all of you." More cheers were raised and the crowd soon afterwards dispersed. OTHER ARRIVALS.

By the same train 51 non-commissioned officers and men r-ached V arrington, being attached to the King's Liverpool Regiment, the Leinstsrs, and the South Lancashires, their time having expired. They left South Africa several weeks ago, and came to England on the as. Montrose, reaching Southamp- ton on Sunday. The men, who disembarked on Monday and left for Warrington in charge of Ser- geants Price and Dryden, belong to several t.iwns. CONGREGAT 10Is!AL UNION.

div.head: Professor Massie Denounces the Education Bill.
div.p: Professor Massie Denounces the Education Bill.

The Congreszational Union of Englull and Wales resumed ita sittings on Thursday at .the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London. Professor Massie (Oxford), in moving a resolution condemning the Education Bill, said the Bill would not further education. It wouli set it back. The Bill was inadequate, undemocratic, retrograde, sectarian, and unjust. The farcical pretence of public control would lull to sleep the a wakening popular interests in edema- Von. If the Bill was not sectarian it would nct relegate education to those who put sect first and education a bad second. (Applause). The Government was stirring up a war at home over this question, Talk about a garrison of 100,0C° men for South Africa. To endeavour to suppress the ow routs of this Bill the Government could gather 100,000 Deans of St Paul! and Cecile; numberless like the sands of the seashore, and yet they would not prevail. (Laughter and applause). Many years ago his (the speaker's) father's property was seized because he refused to pay the old Church rate and if this new rate was levied he (Professor Massie would not be unworth y of his father. (Loud applause) Mr A E Hutton, M.P., seconded, and the resolution was adopted. TWENTIETH CENTURY FUND. Mr Albmt Spicer reported on WI Twentieth Century Fund. He said the central fund amounted to £82,437, which together with bank interest made a total of £83,121. Tne organisations which had benefited by the fund included the London Missionary Society, the Colonial Missionary Society, the Pastors' Retiring Fund, and the new Superannuation Fund.

div.head: MONO-RAIL EXPRESS.
div.p: THE MONO-RAIL EXPRESS.
Work to be Started at Warrington Shortly.

The construction of the mono-rail between Manchester and Liverpool to which the Board of Trade's formal consent has been givea is now within measurable die,- tance.A start will probably be soon made at Warrington, where the generating staton is to be built, and plans for a section in the open country on each side of that town are expected to be finished this week. It is possible that work will also shortly be begun outside the thickly populated districts of Salford and Liverpool, but the construct:on of the Warrington section will be pushed on as rapidly as possible in order that the new system may be fully tested, and That experiments may be msde with the cars which Mr Behr has designed for usa on the line. It is not intended to at present ask the public for Capital, the promoters, who are already assured of sufficient money, holding that it will be he'ter to com- plete the line and show its profit-making capacity b-fore giving the general public an opportunity to subscribe.

- Alteration to the Royal Court Hotel. At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr Charles White (in the chair) and other /magistrates, Mr Browne said he was instructed by Mr Hepherd, the owner of the Royal Court Hotel, Rylands-street, to apply for plans to ba passed for the alteration of the house in consequence of the widening of Bridge-street. This was a matter which had come about through no fault of Mr Hep- herd, but was entirely for the conTenisnce of the town. He had met the Corporation and the adjoin- ing owners, and they had come to terms with regard tolthe different rights of light and land with the result that the end piece abutting into Bridge- street was to be taken down for ab3ut ten feet and that portion put on the sine, making a frontage to both Bridge-street and Rylands- street. Plans had been drawn up by Messrs W and Owen, and Mr Seger Owen wss present to make any explanation which the magistrates mipht deem desirable. There were to be no more rooms in the house with the exception that a lavatory w3uld be provided on the ground floor, a convenience which at present did not exist. The Town Clerk, Mr J Lyon Whittle, was present to support the applica- tion. The present licensee,Mr Wright., had had the house since 1880 and the owner was giving him a further lease, with a promise that he would not ncrease the rent.—The Chief Constable said the alteration would be a great improvement to both the house and the neighbourhood. It would ease that corner for traffic, a consummation which was devoutly to be wished for at the present time, in consequence of the trains.—The Chairman asked whether there would be any room for bar loiterers in the front ,—The Chief Constable replied in the negative, and said be would see to that.—Tbe ap plication was granted.
