div.head: ALLEGED WRONGFUL DISMISSAL. Action by a vVarrington Works Manager.
div.p: ALLEGED WRONGFUL DISMISSAL. Action by a vVarrington Works Manager.
Hearing at Liverpool Assizes.
[By Our Own Reporter.] . LIVERPOOL, WEDNR3DAY•

Shortly after four o'clock this afternoon,the hear- ing was commenced at Liverpool A3SiZB9, before Mr Justice Walton and a jury, of an interest- ing action brought by Mr Richard Wilson Smith, of 139, Wilderspool-road,Warrington, for several years manager of the wire-rope department at Messrs W D Houghton and Sons' works at Sankey Bridges, against his employer Mr. W D. Houghton,for alleged wrongful Idismissal. From the particulars of the claim it appeared that the plaintiff was under an agreement, dated 4th June, 1897, inter alia, to be employed as manager of the wire rope department in the defendant's busi- ness for 7 years from the 14th May, 1897 and hence- forth until the agreement should be determined at any time after the first five years by either party giving to the other three months'notice in writing, or by payment of three months', salary in lieu of euch notice, and it was further agreed that the plaintiff should receive a weekly salary of £3 4s The plaintiff alleged that in breach of the agree- ment, defendant wrongfully dismissed him on the 31st, December, 1901, that he suffered damage and he claimed £1.30. The special damages were loss of salary, 33 weeks at £3 48 per week, £lO5 12s. The defence was that defendant (Mr W D Houghton) did not break the as'- cement and did not dismiss the as alleged, and it was contended that by the agreement the plaintiff agreed t keep a proper super- vision over the defendant's workmen and to diligently and faithfully observe and carry out all the ins•ructions which he should receive and to honestly and diligently perform all the duties required of such manager to the utmost of his skill and kuo.vledge and manage the same in such a manner as to render the position as profitable as possible. It was an implied term of the agreement that the plaintiff should not incapacitate hinocelf by ' drunkenness in the performance of his duties. The plaintiff broke the agreement by coming to work on I several occasions, and especially on the 30th December last, in such a condition of drunkenness as to render him incapacitated and unable to perform his duties and by leaving his work at 11.30 a.m. without leave,and with- out having made any arrangements for the supervision of the workmen or for the other duties he had to perform, whereupon the defendant dismissed him from his em- ployment ; which was the dismissal complained of. The defendant contended that the plaintiff did not suffer any such damage as alleged. Me F Cuthbert Smith Zinstructed by Mr T S Steel of I Warrington), appeared for the plaintiff and Mr digby ' Swift (instructed by Messrs W D Jeans and Son), for the defendant,

div.head: – • COUNSEL'S OPENMP STATEMENT.
div.p: - • COUNSEL'S OPENMP STATEMENT.

Addressing the jury on behalf of the plaintiff, Mr Cuthbert Smith made an elaborate opening statement. This was a case he said, which to hie client was a very serious and a very painful one. The plaintiff was now 60 years of age ana prior to entering Mr Efoughton'e employment be was 28 years at Meesrs Wright's Wire Ropery at Birmingham. Although the defendant had seen fit to put upon the record of that case a charge of drunkenness, and of drunkenness so great as to incapacitate the plaintiff from fulfilling his duties, yet Mr Smiide came before them as a gentle- man who had been in the emplos ment of One firm for 28 years. After that, the plaintiff entered the employ- ment of Messrs Brown's at Liverpool, and was there four years before he was manager of the defendant's workg. He (Mr Cuthbert Smith) was not going to dis- guise the fact from the jury—be did not think it would be right—that the plaintiff while in the employment of Messrs Brown's, had a charge of drunkeuness preferred egraintt him. The plaintiff had Mr Houghton' a in view, and although Messrs Brown's were pre- pared to take him back, he went to Mr Houghton's works. It was to wares the close of the year 1896 that the plaintiff entered the defendant's employ as manager of a wire-rope department which Mr Heughten contemplated starting. Tee plaintiff super- intende 1 the laying down of the plant, and in 1897 an agreement was coma to between the plaintiff and defendant. Under the agreement, the plaintiff tress employed as manager of the wire-rope department. Counsel proceeded to reed several clauses of toe agreement and quoted the one alluded te above with reference to the termination of the agretment. It was a curious c^-incident, he remarked, that the five years mentioned in the agreement would in the ordinate, course of events have expired that dee (May 14th). Therefore, unless the plaintiff had done something to werrant hisinstent eiemissal,the defendant had no right to dismiss the plaintiff as he Gild on the 30th December last year. The plaintiff supervised the erection of the whole of the plant and when the works were complete he was appointed manager. Some time afterwards,a Mr Dixon was intreduced into the business. Mr Dixon, so the plaintiff understood, was engagea as traveller and as a business roan coanected with the firm. About the end ef last year it was ascertained that the wire-rope business was not paying as well as it bad been 'Joke; previously. In July of the same year it was true that the plaintiff had been suspended for a week by his employers, but ha was allowed to resume work and after that date no complaints were made against him. At the conference which took place with reference to the financial working of the rope department, the plaintiff !gave it as his opinion that the reason th 3 department , was not paying was owing to them selling the goods under the cost of production. Whatever might be the reason, the plaintiff said he ceuld not make his depart- ment do any better and there wasn't any suggestion that the plaintiff was neglecting the business or that he was reepensiblio for the state of affairs existing. On the 30th December, which was the first day of °peeing the works after the Christmes holidays, the plaintiff entered the works at 9 o'clock in the morning in the ordinary way. He had been suffering from the after effects of influeeza all through December and WAS not well on the 30ch Dicember. Neveitheless be went to his work and staved there until five minutes to twelve, conducting the basiness of the firm in the usual way and without any complaints whatever. Be went home and lay on the couch, and as it was noticed by the family that the plaintiff was too ill to go back to work, the son sent a note to Mr Dixon explaining that they had persuaded the plaintiff to stay at home owing to his illness, but hoping be would be well enough to come on the following morning. The letter sent by the son was as follows : Mr Dixon : Father not being so well when be came to dinner I persuaded him to stay at home. If there is anything particular von want to know about and will send ms word perhaps I could let you know. Father and I hope myself will be down first thing in the morn- ing. Hoping you will not be put about at my father's absence and that you will have a look round the works —Richard Smith jun. The son was one of the invalids in the house and the note was taken by one of the daughters. The same nieht Mr Dixon wrcte to the pleiritiff as follows i—it De tr Sir, I regret that as a matter of duty I am compelled to give you notice that you are suspended from entering the works until I have communicated with Mr Houghton who will decide whether your services will be any longer required." The Clltioll9 fact was that at the same time the note was sent to the plaintiff, a letter was sent to the son discharging bias. Subsequently Mr Houghton sent the following letter to the plaintiff :—" I have been informed that Mr Dixon WAS obliged to suspend you from duty ia consequence of you having entered the works on the morning of the 30th December, suffering tender the influence of intcxicants, and that you after- wards left the works during working hours without making arrangements for some com- petent workman to take the responsibility. You were recently suspended, and I cannot do other- wise than inform you that you arc dismissed from my service." Counsel proceeded to explain in detail the actions of Ike plaintiff on the day in ques- tion. During the preceding night Mr.. Smith had been ill and be left home shertly before nine o'clock, having bad One of the lightest of breakfasts. He called at the Sloop Hotel and had one glass of whisky in some tea. That woul I ceetainly not m‘lte anyone in the coadition described in tee letter. There were men to the Sloop Hotel at the time, and the barmaid who served the plaintiff would be called and would say he had only one glass of whisky. There was not a traei of intcxication about him and ho went abeut his work in the regular and usual way. During the course of the morning one of hie Majesty's Inspectors came in to test certain wire ropes that were being made for Messrs Vickers, Maxim and Company. Mr Smith was called up and spoke to the inspector about the quality of the rope. If the plaintiff had entered the works on the 30th December suffering under intoxication be was hardly the person Mr Dixon would have called up to discuss the quality of ropes with the Government inspector. Plaintiff left the works shortly before twelve o'clock and on going out he met Mr Jefferson, a plumber, whom he did not know, and delivered a message to him which his son had brought from Birmingham. Mr Jefferson would be able to tell the Court that there was not a trace of drink upon the plaintiff. The men to wham the plaintiff gave orders would be able to say that the work was sufficient for them to go on with and Mr Smith's presence was not nearled 1 for the purpose of enabling them te go on with their work. The plaintiff might have been guilty of a techni- cal error in leaving the works without asking somebody's , permiaion but he did not imperil his master's interests. I t If the defendant was unable. to put it any higher than that, he did not think the jury would consider that sufficient to warrant him in discharging the plaintiff at a moment's notice.

THE PLAINTIFF IN THE BOX. Richard Wilson Smith, the plaintiff, said he was 60 Tears IDE ace that day. For 28 years he was employed with Messrs J and Edwin Wright wire.rope mann- facturers,of Birmingiaam,and he was manager for them

div.p: THE EXAM IN ER FRIOA V MAY 16, 1902.

for 26 years. In October 1892, witness went to Messrs Brown's at Sink flail, Liverpool. The reason he left the last named place was through intoxication. He had been out of employment some months when he I obtained employment at the defendant's premises to- wards the end of 1896. The wire-rope business was al new branch entireli and witnesa superintended the erection of the plant and on the fourth of June in the following year he entered into the agreement whititi had bsen read. Na complaints were made against hint of insobriety or inattlndance up to July 2nd last year. On that date witness was suspended for being intoxi- cated, bat he restarted work on the following week. From that date up to the 30th December no charge was made against him. At a conference held at the works he was told ttat the wire rope department was not pay- ing and witness informed those present (Messrs W D Houghton. John 114ughton, Ernest Houghton, 13 Dixon and Hill) that they were selling the ropes uarler cost. In November witness was laid up for three weeks with in- fluenza and suffered from the after affects of it for some time. Monday, the 30th of Dmember WAS the first day of re-opening the works after the Christmas holidays. Witness corroborated dounsal's state nent as to calling at the Sloop Hotel on his way to the works and having whisky and tea. He felt rather weak and he thought it would do bit good. He received orders from Mr. Dixon and pave the men instructions for getting the work in hand. He was present when the Government Inspector arrived and spoke to him about the quality of the reNs. Witness went home early betauae he Was anxious about his children who were ill, and he told the lod,gernan he was going on a little private business. He had given suffi ;blot work to the men to last them the whole day. He had a small whisky at the Sloop on returning home. He found that dinner Was not ready and he went out to get his hair cut. Whilst out he visited the Black Horse, and there had two glasses of bitter beer. He then went home for dinner and afterwards fell asleep on the couch. It was an accident that he slept so long, for he intended to go back to his work. He asked his son whether he had written to the works, and he replied that he had not done so. Ells sou then dispatched the letter which had been read. He saw Mr Dixon with reference to the letter he had sent in reply, and told Mr Dixon that he only had "two soots "oh whisky, and Mr Dixan said he did not notice it. _

Cross-examined by Mr Swift: He had trouble with Messrs Wright of Birmingham cu two occasions about drink but he did not leave them on that account. When 1 he h indsd in his notice one of tee partners said " I am very sorry." He left at the r?quest of a friend namod Mr Brown who was starting a works at Liverpool. He was dismissed by Messrs Brown for drunkenness. Wnen he saw Mr Houghton about introducing a wiro ropery at his works, Mr Houghton sake I him why he was leaving and he replied " Brawn wants me to be a tee- totaler." Tenre had never been any camplaint made against him at Houghton' except that of drunkenness In July, 1893, Dixon got hnld of him by the collar ' whilst he was putting a belt on. Witness told him that if he did not lcose him he would hit him (Mr Dixon). Dixon told him that he was drunk and witness denied it Witness remembered an incident at Reek Bear bridge in connection with the loading of a large coil Of rope for the Bengal Railway Company.lle admit'ed that after the wcrk was done he went and got drunk with the men,bat it was after working hours. It was the biggest job they bad done up to that time, and they were celebrating it. (Laughter.) He admitted that he was taken home in a cab. The work was finished about seven o'clock at night. He was not so drunk that Connor's refused th let him have a cat. It was untrue to say that a man named Burke had taken him to Connor's for a cab.
At thl3 stage th 9 Court adj)urnod until the following day.

Black Bear wharf job got drunk that night. Mr Smith went home in a can. fie ciuld not tell whether they could walk all righr. (Laughter.) John Gough, smother workman, stated that plaintiff seerntd as usual on the morning of December 30th..
Mr Smith : flas anyone spoken to you about giving evidence here 2 Witness : Mr Smith.

Re-examined : The defendsnt bad not tried to induce him not to give evidence. No one connected with the firm had spoksn to him about his evidence. Mr Smith: It is my mistake. Mr Swift : It is a sort of thing which ought not to be misunderstood.

Mrs Llewellyn. wife of the licensee of the Sloop Hotel said she took charge of the bar about eleven o'clock on the morale.: of December 30th. Plaietiff came in and had a small wbialty. ay His Lordship : It was some time aFtemards before she heard the plaintiff had been dismissed. By Mr _Smith : Ha was vile sober when ha came in. . .

Annis Smith, daughter of the plaintiff, said she re- membered her father coming in for lunch at noon on December 30. th. Her father was quite sober. Be had coffee and duck.:She did not give him coffee for the pur- pose of making him sober. Later in the afternoon she took a lettor, writtm by her brother, to Mr Dixon, and aftet reading it, Mr Dixon said he was afraid the a atter had gons too far. This concluded the plaintiff's cw. THE DEFENCE.

Mr Rigby Swift, in addressing toe Ceurt for the d fence, said the jury had one question and one question only to decide and that question was whether the de- fendant was justified in dismissing Mr Smith from his service in consequence- of the ceeditiou he was in through drink on the 30th December. Not oaly must the jury consider what was his condition on that date but they must have regard to what had been the con- ditien under which he had been working for some time past. Although they might reasonably say that one isolated instance of a man taking too much drink was not suffilieut to justify the breaking off of such an agree- mane, when they found that that man had from time to time been giving way to intemperance, they would recognise that some step must be taken, Rue) this kind of wing put a stop to. The plaintiff admitted that he had been lo the habit of given way to intemperance. When at Birmingham, there were t wo.occasions at least whieh he admittedon which he got into trouble in noose- quince of drink, although he was not dismissed because of thoei troubles. Then toe plaintiff went to Mr Brown at Liverpool, and within five tears his engagement was terminated and ho was thrown out of employment because he bad given way to drink. In September he obtained employment from Mr Houghten but he never suggested to Mr Houghton that the cause of his leaving Brown's was because of Jrunkennese. Woilst in 'sir Houghton's ernpley- merit he continued his drinking propensities. H admitted having been drunk at the works on July 2nd and on another occasion outside the works whilst engaged in loading a bergs at the Black Bear bridge. Counsel proceeded to ask the jury to consider the position of the plaintiff whilst in Ws employer's service and the people with whom he got drunk. He was the foreman over the men and was it a proper thing for the plaintiff to get drunk with the men, even after working hours, as he had admitted was the case in the Black Bear incident ? Was that the right line for a man to take who had the supervision of a number of men ? Furthermore, the plaintiff had a number of boys under his charge and these bore had been seat out of the works by the plaintiff for the purpose of bringing in whisky. The plaintiff had to admit that these little peculiarities were not known to his employers. The boys who went for the plairriff's whisky knew that! it had to be kept quiet for if the employers knew there would be un- pleasantness. There Was no doubt that the plaintiff was drank at the works on the 2nd July and in conse- quence ha WWI suspended. Ile was taken on again with a warning that if it occurred again he would be die- misSet From the 2nd July, the plaintiff abandoned the morning drinking, and he (counsel) would think that 993 out of every thnisand would agree that a morning drink was a meet pernicious habit. The plaintiff gave it up until the very morning that Mr Dixon says be foeni him under the influence of drink, that was the 30th December. It was an extraordinary coinci- dence. The very first time that anybody made any sug- gestion about the plaintiff,he had, on his own admission, broken through the good rule he had made and returned to the pernicious habit of morning ii king. The plaintiff might have been able to walk all Ylitt on this very morning, tut he was mudded in his talk and he was foolish, and he was not in a fit condition to go round the works with the inspector, and Mr Dixon had to take his place and conduct the testing of wire in the presence of the inspector. The learned Counsel pro- ceeded to comment on the plaintiff's action in leavieer the works before the proper time, and instead of staying at home, of visiting another public-house and obtaining further drink. He was unable to come to his work in the afternoon and another man had to be temporarily placed in his pesition in order to keep the inert employed. Having regard to what happened on the 2nl July, con eget c )ratended that Mr. Houghton Was jurifiel, and more than justified in dismissing him. WITNESSES FOR THE DEFENCE. ..... .

William Dinkson Ii 'tarifa", the defendant, said in September 1896 plaintiff appli3d to him for a ,sifuttion. Mr. Smith aid not tell him that he had lett Brown's in consNvnes of drink, but gave him the impression that there had bsen some friction. In July last year, plain- tiff wsi suspendili in cormegnenne of lo"ing dronk at the works,hut he was allowed to resume work with a caution. The plaintiff WM a capable workman and there was no reason for dismissing him apart from drunkenness. On the 313 t December, witness went t,4 the works and heard of the incident from Mr Dixon. Ho left the whole of the matter to Mr Dixon failing sure to st Mr Dixon would do what was right.

Cross-examined by Mr Smith : Plaintiff was not led to think he would be able to see him (Mr Houghton through any word of his. Mr Dixon was the chief manager of the rope department. Mr Smith did not tell him that he had left Brown's because they wanted himl to be'a teetotaler. He didn't write to Wright's or Br )wn's with referonce to Smith's charact-r. He knew the man was a capable workman and ha thought ha would suit him for the rope. department. Questioned by His Lordship as to what Smith did say when he applied persoually for the appointment, Mr Houghton said the plaintiff told him there bad been so much friction of late between himself and Mr Brown that he could nct stand it any longer and he had dis- connected himself with Brown's. Ha was quite expeat- ing that Mr Brown would be sending for him again. He did not say he had left Brown's on account of drunken- ness. . .

Robert Dixon, general manager cf the work, said he began his duties at Houghton's on the let January 1897. There had been some friction as to who was in com- mand, owiag to the plaintiff's jealousy. The plaintiff's position was foreman of the rope department. Oa the 30th December he saw plaintiff in the wis,ks and noticed that he was rather muddled owing to drink. He smelled very Strongly. Witness took Smith to the In- spectoe. Ho was still muddled. It ens witness's busi- ness to explain anything to the inspector and to refer to Smith for any information. W tri eqs told Smith what the inspector wanted doing but he did not take any steps to get it done and made a rambling statement to the inspector. Smith was not hopelessly drunk but was under the influence of drink and be smelled etrongly of it. Witness was desirous of looking at Smith's order book but he fount! the foreman's place Inked up at twenty minutes to twelve. lie asked for Smith and limn Ihe had gone. A. man named Speakman was without any instructions as to what he had to do. _ _ .

At this stags the O-o.urt adjourned fcr luncheon. On rest:ening. Mr Dixon continued his evidence and said most of the men before twelve o'clock were waiting for orders when ilo visited the r very. At two o'clock he went to the departrneat again and found that the whole of the machinery was pracsic.ally at a eandetill because the MO9 had had no instructions to go on. Cross-examined : If the plaintiff hod coin I hank in the afternoon in the same condition as he was in the morning, he would nct have discharged him. The reason for Smith's discharge was a joint reason, Ist be- cause he Wa9 meddled in the morning and secondly because he didn't Come bock in the afternoon. Atten- tion having been called by c mos,l to Lho orders written by the plaintiff on the morning of 30th December, witness said they were writrm under the influence of drink. He had seen plaintiff write fairly-well when ha was drunk. The Inspector did not say anything about Smith's condition. Re-examined : It was untrue to suggest that he had got rid of Smith through malice. When he received the letter from Sue son he came to the conclusion that it was the .• same old thin," i.e. that the plaintiff was drinking. George Watson, now occupying Me. Srnith's position, said he and Salida worked together at Brown's and he (Watson) followed him to Houghton's. They were always on friendly terms. Witness formed the opinion that on the morning of December 30th, Smith bad had some drink and more than was good for him. When witneos spoke to plaintiff, Smith was muddled in his talk. He gave witness two Orders which were quite in- consistent. Smith also smelled very strongly. When Smith did cot turn no in ths afternoon witness was appointed temporarily in his place. He had seen him drunk at the works on other occasions. Cross-examined : Witness had not seen Smith drunk at the works since the 2nd July, with the exception of the 30th December. William bingard, a workman, said the plaintiff's con- dition seemed to go worse on the 30th December as the morning advanced. He saw the plaintiff have a spirit drink, and he smelt him of it. He bad a shaky walk. John Whittaker, another workman, sad be was of opinion that Smith was under the influence of drink on December 30tb.Hei.did not walk straight across the yard. Christopher Basketer, stated that he was in the Black Horse on the 30th December when the plaintiff was there drinking. Witness said " Now Wilson Smith let us have you back 'again." He replied No," Witness Could tell by plaintiff's face that the plaintiff had bad too much to drink, (Laughter). Witness weat to the

works and on Watson asking him if he had seen Smith, he replied that he had seen Win in the Black Horse. William Bramhall, warehouse men and storekeeper, said the plaintiff was not in afl state to see the in- spector. He walked unsteadily. James Speakman deposed that he was under the supervision ot Smith and on December 30:h be had two machines stopped. He went to see Smith for orders but could not find him. Teat was shortly before 12 o'clock. Mr Swift then addressed the jury for the defence, and commented upon the fac: that the plaintiff's son bad not been called. Mr Smith said the son wee in court and would have been called but he (counsel) did not think it necessary to call him.
His Lordship decided that the son shnuld go into the witnesi b3x.

• Richard Wilson Smith teen give evidence and said he saw his father when he came in. He was:not under the influence of drink. Cross-examined . fle asked his father • when he came in the second time if he had had drink. Tile reason for the question was that his fattier had been away such a long time, not b scene° he noticed signs of drink upon him. It was after four o'cleck when the plaintiq awoke, that witness advised him to stay indoors. Ele did net so far advise him tiatil he awoke from sleep. Mr Swift then proceeded with his speech and said it was quite clear that the son thought it necessary to ask his father if he had something to drink. The plaintiff's conduct at the dinner time and in the afternoon bore out strongly the opinion formed by Mr Dixon that the man was muddled or under the influence of drink. He stayed away from his work drinking and after Mr Dixon's experience of him on occasions prior to the 2ad July, Mr Dixon was justified in dismissing him from employment. Mr Cuthbert Smith, in addressing the jury on behalf of the plaintiff said he had been able to at once refute the suggestion of Mr Swift with reference to the non- calling of this plaintiff's son b 7 placing him in the box. They saw the young man in the box and he was sure the jury were now glad to have beerd him. The eon cor- roborated the daughter'e statement that the father was perfectly sober and not wider the influence of drink on the 30th D cenibisr. Till jury were encitled to weigh the evidence in the light of probabilities. To Mr Hougnton, the presence or absence of a servant was not a question of very much moment. From his pint of view the whole ctiostion was really a very small one, but to the plaintiff it was of me most serious and vita importance what the result of the verdict was. The plaintiff Was 60 years of age and it WAS common kiowledge that when a men loses his place at 60 years of age it was ex- ceedingly difficult to get any employment at all after- wards. They could realise how much more difficult it would be when his discharge was coupled with the offence of being drunk and utterly unable of attending to his work. If the jury's verdict was against Mr Smith that would be the end of Mr Smith's career. They would therefore see what a very seriono issue it was for the plaintiff. Mr Swift had complained of the plaintiff's son not being called but tie (Mr Cuthbert Smith) would esk why has the Government inspector not beers called by the defendant ? Teat gentleman was a perfectly in lependent gentleman and would have been ab!ei to speak of the condition of the plaintiff on the morning in question. Every effort had been made on the plaintiff's part to get him to give evidence, but the defendant had mile no such attempt to obtain an independent Wi71931. Every witness called by the defendant had been witnesses from the works. fie hoped the jury would not forget the eviaence of Jeff cane, who was an entirrly independent witnees,and who et tted that the plaintiff was not affected by drinking 03 the morn- ing in question. ' The question for the jury was whether the plaintiff was or WAS not capable of doing his work. If he was then the defendant had no tight to dismiss him. He left the case with absolute confidence in the hands of the jury knowing that they would weign fairly the evidence and feeling assured that no jury of res- pectable men would ever blast the career of a man on the class of evie'ence which had been brougnt before them.

His Lordship summed up at length, and pointed out that the jury must decide what amounted to miscon- duct ; and whether there was such misconduct as war- ranted the defendant in putticg the man out of his Ler- vice at once. Alludia4 to the plaintiff's condition, his Lordship said the plaintiff seemed to have been able to give orders on the dat3 in question. So far as his memory and competence to give orders and the under- standing of the diameter of wire were concerned, it appeared that he was able Co attend to his duties. The plaintiff's explanation cf his absence in the afternoon was that he went co sleep on the couch after dinner and overslept hirnsslf. If such a mistake bid been made it was quite uatural for Mr Dixon, on receiving the note, to jump to the co.aclusioa that it was the came old story of the plaintiff having got drunk. He asked the jury to say " yes" or " " whether the defendant was justi- fied in dismissing the plaintiff: • THE VERDICT.
The jury. after a s-h—or—t cOn—e-uitaii;noreturnel a vordiet fcr the defendant.

div.head: Second Day's Proceedings.
div.p: Second Day's Proceedings.
LIVERPOOL TIIUBSDAf. The plaintiff again entered the bpx on the opening of the 3econd day's proceedings. _ _ .

Cross-examined by Mr S wift, witne,s admitted that he came to the works drunk on the 2nd July. A police- man was threatened to be sent for nut witness went home When he went to the works later on, he was told they would take him on again bat it would be the last chance He knew that if he got drunk again he would be dis- missed. That was in working hours. From the let July to September he was a teetotaler but he ceased being so about September. He admitted sending a boy named Howarth out of the works/ for whisky. He also sent other boys under his charge for whisky. He gave them a note to go out. Asked if it was a proper thitig to Slad boys out for whisky during business hours, witness replied that it was better than going out himself for it. From July to Dicember be never sent a bey out , for whisky. Oa the morning of December 30, witness was not muddled. Be had only had one glass of whisky. It did not make him muddled and foolish. When the Government inspector visited the works witness did ratt tell the inspector that he (the inspector) did not know how to test a rope. When he went lo speak to Forster, one of the workmen, he almost thought he asked Forster to have a drink. Forster was crossing the yard at the time. It would he about 5 minutes to 12. On going home he called at the Sloop Hotel and had a special whisky. He afterwards had two bitters at the Black Horse. Alter dinner he went to lie , down as his head was bad, but it was not owing to the drink, although he admitted it was a curious mixture he had had. He saw Mr Dixon on the fo'bw- ing day, after he had been suvended. He believed if he had seen Mr Houghton things would have been different. Mr Houghton °always appeared to him to be a gentleman. He had seen it printed on the firm's circular that Mr Dixon wadirector of the works' department, but be was not aware that Mr Dixon was over him.

Re•examined by Mr Smith From July he en- deavoured to turn over a new leaf. It was before July when be was sending out boys for dritk. After July his office in the workroom was pulled dowo. There was only one occasion when he went home in a cab and that was the incident at the Black B^ar in February. It wab after working hours. EVIDENCE FOR THE PLAINFIFF.

Fro3erick Thomas Jefforson, master plumber and painter, Liverpool-road, ',Farrington, said ho first met the plaintiff on the Mond ty following Caristrais Day. He met him near the lodge of Anima Houghton's works about three minutes bgore 12 o',;lock. Plaintiff gave him a message from Birmingham which plaintiff's son had brought. Plaintiff did not appear to be under the influence of drink. He did not notice him particularly as he had not met him before.

His Lordship : Was there anything in his minter to sueeest that he had been drinking ? Witness : Nothing at all. Elizabeth Smith, wife of the plaintiff, corroborated her buatand's statement with referencs ti his conduct during Christmas week. His Lordship Wi.s hs drinking during Christmas week ?

Witness : Ni, In answer to questions by Mr Smith, the witness said her husband had been suffering from influenzs, and they had a sick house at 'Christmas week. Plaintiff had drink before he left the house on the morning of December 30th. Ha was complaining of his head. She did not see him when he came in to dinner. Cross-examined lov Mr Rigby Swift: She had not seen him incapable owing to urink, but she had seen him sometimes "jolly " and sometimes " cross " owing to drink.

Betty Llewellyn, dads:liter of the licensee of the Sloop Hotel said she was in charge of the bar on the mornin, of the 30th December. She remembered the plaintiff coming to the house jolt before niae o'clock. He had a glass of whisky and drank it with tea. That was all he bad. There were acme other men there and he said "Come along chaps it is time to bo off." Cross-examined by Mr It Swift; She did not see him when be came ia at noon.

Frederick V Childs. shingler in the employ of Messrs Monks, Hall and Company but former;y in the employ of the defendant said he remembered the rt-opening of Houghton's works after the Christmas holidays and saw Mr Smith immediately after nine o'clock on the morn- ing of December 30th, with reference to some work. Mr Smith gave him the orders clearly. Asked if he was a teetotaler witness said he had taken three small bottles of stout in 3k years. (Lsuuhter). Mr &rash was quite sober on the morning of the 30th De:ember. At the Black Bear incident there was some drink brought on the job just as the coil was nearly bacied in the boat. Mr Smith sent for the beer. - -

R;;;;Mi-xied : He had never seen 6.1 r Smith under the intlcence of drink at the works. He had never told a men named Cooper that " the old man (meaning Smith) was as drunk as he could be." He remembered having some words win Smith but he did not tell Burke and Cooper that Smith was boozed and did not know what he was doing. In answer to his Lordship, why witness was dis- discharged, be replied that he did not know the reason. He had just been outside te thd urinal and was told he had better accept a week's notice. A man named Watson who succeeded Smith told him that. He be- lieved the real reason of his dismissal was malice.

Benry Craske employed for four year and seven months at MC3911113-eighton's Ttia th, plaintiff came ro him in the works on tie morning of Dvernber 30th and gave him his orders. Witness never suspected that the plaintiff had been drinking at all. Cross-examined : Witness bad gone out of the works and fetched whisky and beer for the plaintiff. That was six or eight months previous to December. Re fancied there would have been a row if Mr:Dixon and Mr Houghton had been aware of the practice. John Thomas Mather,formerly in the employ of defen- dant,gave corroborative evidencsas to the plaintiff being able to do his work. Cross-examined : Mr Watson was appointed to succeed Me Smith when he did not come to his work in the afternoon of D,cember 30th. Witness left Hough- ton's of his own accoid. John Westero,a wire strand spina, r at the defendant's works gave evidence as to receiving instructions from plaintiff on the morning of the 30th December. In answer to his Lordship witness said there was nothing in his appearance or manner to indicate that he bad been drinking. , Re-examined by Mr Swift : Moat of the men on the

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
PROVIDENCE _FREE HOSPITAL, ST.. HELENS.

The annual meeting of subscribers and friends of the Providence Free Hospital was held on Thursday night. Councillor j B Leach presided, and in proposing the adoption of the annual report referred to the large sums of money which would be required to pay for the build- ing of the boundary wall and the payment of Corporation charges for street expenses. The hospital had been worked in a most satisfactory manner, and the accounts were more favoureble than in the previous vesr. The perinv a week collectors had brought in 84,036 pennies—£350 3.. id. The laundry receipts were exceedingly good. With the Resistance of some of the old patients, who gave their labour for a few hours a day,ths grounds of the hospital were gradu- ally being laid out.--31r C D Fothergin seconded, and referred to the good work of the sistere.—The report and ba'ance•sheet were adopted. Lord Gorard was re-Aected president, and all the officers were re-elected.

div.head: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES.
div.p: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES.

The regular sailings of the steamers of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Co to and from Liverpool and Llandudno and the Straits have vastly increased the popularity if North Wales al a holiday resort,seeing that, the destination can be reached with such facility and in such comfort. For tho Whit-week holidays special sailings are announced, and, given fine weather, there should be no more popular trips than those by the St Tudno, St Elvies, or Snowdon. The S. Tudno and St. Elvies will sail on Saturday morning and afternoon respectively. On Whit Sunday the sailings will be St Tudno an.l Sno wdon in the morn- ing, passengers joining the St. Tadao either at Llan- dudno or Beautnaris. On Whit Monday morning S. Elvies will steam to Llandudno and Flolyhead (due back in the evening), sod tha St. Tudno on the orrlinary run. On Twsday there will be an early boat from Llandudno duo in Liverpool in the forenoon. Subsequently during the season the S. Tudno takes tip tho regular sailing for North Wales.

Brunner, Mond and Company. —Another Handsome Dividend., On Wednesday, Sir John Brunner presided over a meeting of the directors of Messrs Brunner, Mond, and Company, Limited, held in the Board Room at the Winnington Works, near Northwich. After considering the workings of the company for the year ended March 31st last, it was decided to recommend to the shareholders, at their meeting on the 28th lust, the declaration of a dividend of 32i per cent. on ordinary shares and 7 per cent. on pre- ference shares for the year. It was also decided to carry £60,000 to the suspense fund, to write off £2500 on the patents, and to carry forward to the reserve fund £37,000.

. . Mr William Mather, t P, presiding at the annual meeting of the Castner-Kellner Alkali Company held in London, on Thursday,said at last they were out of the wood. They had been ham- pered, not to say persecuted, by other competitors, and during the last five years had been in almost a constant state of litiga- tion. They had now got free of these difficulties, and their patents were intact. The prospects of their enterprise were never so good as now, and it only required that bleaching powder should be ap- plied more largely to industrial purposes to place them in a state of great prosperity, The report was adopted.—ln reply to a question from a share- holder as to the absence of Sir H Rome, the chair- man said he was restored to health, but would have to be extremely careful about venturing out for some tim9 to c)me. His presence and services were highly appreciated on the board.

The "Daily NOW 9 " atates that the result of the Bury election has, it is cynically said, had a withering efloet, on the demand for peerages, which up to that point had been an extreme brisk and promising market. One or two candidates who were well in the running have had reason to believe,tbat peeragEs involving an election are “off." The Governor of the Isle of Men, Lord Henniker has issued to the Maox Legislature a statement of the film- dim p„iti„ a the wand. The revenue for the year ended 30th March wee £79,832, being £12,957 less than the previous year. The principal decreases are in the Spirit and tobacco duties. The expenditure was £75,542 being an increase of £1,444. The Government debt is £264.452. The revenue for the current year is estimated at £0,300, and the expenditure at £75,170.

POLICE CASE.

At ths Earlestown POiled Station on Monday morning before Mr J IV Emmett, John Mallitt was charged with being drunk and disorderly in &tries- town on Saturday,aud was flue.! 2s 6d and costs. In default of payment he was sent to goal for 7 days.

div.head: BOWLING HANDICAP AT EABLESTOWN.
div.p: BOWLING HANDICAP AT EABLESTOWN.

A handicap at bowls in connectiori with the Vii- duct Institute Bowling Club was held on the club ground on Saturday afternoon. There were 44 entries, the competition being for Mr Thorp's annual prize and the entrance fees. The first prize was taken by Mr J Pope, 2nd J Gee, 3rd J Clough.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARY.

The weekly melting ot tne 1.0.G.T. was held at the Wargravell on Nionday night, a good num- ber being present, Bro. Cutler C.T. presided. Some interesting readingi were given by Bros. Woods, Clarke and Newman. Two II3W members were initiated. The report of the convention showed that the order was doing goo I work and that its membership was largely increasing. BENEFIT CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN.

On Thursday evening a concert, for the benefit of Mr E Roberts, was given in the Town Hall, Earles- town. There was a very good audience, and an excellent array of artistes had given their services The programme was varied man included quartettes by Misses Watkins and Evans. Messrs Powell and Edwards, songs by Misi Jennie Roberts, Miss Griffiths, Miss Watkins, Mr F Edwards and humor- ous songs by Mr Charles Neary of St Helens. During the interval a vote of thanks to the artistes was propoied by Mr J H Profit and seconded by Mr E T Evans.

div.head: SERIOUS F ARAI FIRE AT NEWTON.
div.p: SERIOUS F ARAI FIRE AT NEWTON.

Soon after midnight on Tuesday, a fire broke out on the farm occupied by Mr Gilb..rt in Ashton- road, Newton, resulting in the complete demolition of a large barn and its contents. Mr Gilbert's son was awakened by the glare from the flames, and jumping out of bed alarmed the household, after- wards rushing to the works of:Messrs McOorquodale and Compan3 for the fire engine. After a short delay the brigade was got together, and arrived on the scene, but the flames had got such a firm hold of the building that they were unable to cope with them, and the fire was allowed to burn itself out only the bare walls being left standing. Some valuable farming inplementa and machinery stored in' the barn were destroyed, but all were insured. The damage is estimated at £7OO. It is supposed the fire was caused by tramps sleeping on the premises.

EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. The special ear ViCes in coanection with the anniver- sary of the above school were held on Sunday. The weather was quite in keeping with the occasion,and there was consequently large congregations at each of the three services. The preacher for the day wa9 the Rev T Wynne Jones of London, and formerly of Earlestown. and he delivered a coupla of excellent dizcourses. A .tpecial choir of well trained children was arranged in front of the ros- trum and they sang in an admirable manner the various hymns allotted to them, Mr T Clare officiat- ing as conductor. In the afternoon the sacred cantata" The Eastern Star " was submitted by the choir and children. Mr G W Kidd presiding at the organ and Mr Clare conducting. The principal soloist were Misses Adams, D Roberts, M Barr, Holliday, Messrs R A Robinson, Webster,and Twem- low. The collections throughout the day amounted to £7l.
